employment-law/alabama/overtime-rights.summary: Alabama does not have a general state overtime law, so overtime rights generally come from the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). Covered, nonexempt employees must receive at least one and one-half times their regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, rather than overtime simply for working a long day, weekend, or holiday. Coverage, exemptions, and the calculation of the regular rate determine whether additional pay is owed.

sections.heading: Which Alabama employees have overtime rights?

facts.label: Federal coverage
facts.value: The FLSA covers employees through covered enterprises or their own interstate-commerce work. Enterprise coverage generally includes businesses with at least $500,000 in annual sales or business, as well as specified institutions and public agencies regardless of business volume. A smaller employer can still have individually covered workers. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 203(s), 207(a).

facts.label: Exemptions
facts.value: Executive, administrative, and professional exemptions depend on applicable regulatory requirements, not job titles alone. Salary payment by itself does not eliminate overtime rights; these exemptions generally involve duties and compensation tests, subject to exceptions. — 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1); 29 C.F.R. Part 541.

facts.label: Hours counted
facts.value: Work the employer permits can count even when it was not requested. An advance-approval rule does not erase the obligation to pay for compensable overtime actually worked. — 29 C.F.R. §§ 785.11–785.13.

rows: At least 1.5 times the regular rate after 40 hours worked in a workweek.

These days do not automatically require premium pay under the FLSA.
Qualifying state and local government employers may provide compensatory time instead of cash overtime under statutory conditions, at 1.5 hours per overtime hour.

facts.label: Lawsuit deadline
facts.value: An FLSA unpaid-overtime action generally must begin within two years after the claim accrues, extended to three years for a willful violation. A Wage and Hour Division complaint does not itself stop this lawsuit clock. — 29 U.S.C. § 255(a); U.S. Department of Labor, Fact Sheet #44.

facts.label: Available recovery
facts.value: Employees can recover unpaid overtime and an equal amount in liquidated damages, plus reasonable attorney fees and costs. A court may reduce or deny liquidated damages if the employer proves statutory good faith and reasonable grounds. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 216(b), 260.

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: The FLSA prohibits discharge or discrimination because an employee files a protected complaint or participates in covered proceedings. Remedies can include reinstatement, lost wages, and an equal amount in liquidated damages. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 215(a)(3), 216(b).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alabama
bullets: The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division receives and investigates FLSA overtime complaints involving Alabama employment. Its national telephone number is 1-866-487-9243.

FLSA private lawsuits may be brought in a federal or state court of competent jurisdiction. Alabama has Northern, Middle, and Southern federal judicial districts. — 29 U.S.C. § 216(b); 28 U.S.C. § 81.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alabama
bullets: Does a 12-hour shift automatically earn overtime? No. The ordinary FLSA rule is based on more than 40 hours worked in a workweek, although special statutory arrangements apply to certain workers.

Can private employers substitute future time off? Generally, they cannot substitute time off in a later workweek for required FLSA cash overtime. The statutory compensatory-time exception concerns qualifying public employers.
Does paid vacation count toward 40 hours? Generally, paid time not worked does not count toward the FLSA overtime threshold.
Can an employee agree to waive overtime? An individual agreement generally cannot waive the FLSA’s overtime requirements.

employment-law/alaska/family-medical-lea.summary: Alaska has a state family-leave law for qualifying public employees, while the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) covers eligible employees of covered public and private employers. Alaska’s public-employee law provides up to 18 workweeks for qualifying family or medical reasons, with different measuring periods depending on the reason; federal FMLA generally provides 12 workweeks in 12 months. These are job-protected leave rights, not a general guarantee of paid wages during an absence.

facts.label: State law and coverage
facts.value: The Alaska Family Leave Act appears in AS 39.20.305–39.20.315 and applies to qualifying public employment. It is not a general family-leave mandate for private employers; statutory employer and employee eligibility requirements apply. — AS 39.20.305–39.20.315

facts.label: Employee eligibility
facts.value: An employee qualifies through employment for at least 35 hours a week for at least six consecutive months, or at least 17.5 hours a week for at least 12 consecutive months, immediately preceding the leave. — AS 39.20.305

facts.label: Medical reasons
facts.value: Qualifying reasons include the employee’s own serious health condition and caring for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition. Routine illnesses do not automatically meet the statutory definition. — AS 39.20.305; AS 39.20.315

facts.label: Job protection
facts.value: The state law provides return-to-work protection following qualifying leave. Entitlement to leave and restoration remains subject to the statute’s conditions. — AS 39.20.305

facts.label: Employer coverage
facts.value: Private employers generally qualify with at least 50 employees during 20 or more workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Public agencies are covered regardless of size, but individual employee eligibility requirements still apply. — 29 U.S.C. § 2611; 29 C.F.R. § 825.108

facts.label: Pay, insurance, and overlapping leave
facts.value: FMLA leave is generally unpaid, although qualifying paid leave may run concurrently. Group health coverage continues on the same terms. State and federal leave can run concurrently when the absence qualifies under both laws; their maximum amounts are not automatically added together. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 2612(d), 2614(c); 29 C.F.R. § 825.701

facts.label: Federal lawsuit deadline
facts.value: An FMLA action generally must be filed within two years after the last alleged violation, or three years for a willful violation. Remedies can include lost compensation, interest, liquidated damages, equitable relief, and attorney fees. — 29 U.S.C. § 2617

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alaska
bullets: The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division receives FMLA complaints involving employment within its enforcement jurisdiction.
Federal FMLA civil actions may be brought in a federal or state court of competent jurisdiction. — 29 U.S.C. § 2617(a)(2)
Alaska executive-branch employees’ state leave administration involves their employing agency and the Alaska Division of Personnel and Labor Relations.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alaska
bullets: Does every Alaska worker receive 18 weeks? No. That entitlement comes from the public-employee law and depends on statutory eligibility.
Is family leave necessarily paid? No. Job protection and wage payment are separate questions; accrued paid leave or another applicable benefit may provide pay.
Can federal leave cover a parent’s serious illness? Yes, for an eligible employee caring for a qualifying parent with a serious health condition.
Can an employer punish an employee for using FMLA rights? Federal law prohibits interference with FMLA rights and prohibited retaliation. — 29 U.S.C. § 2615

employment-law/alaska/overtime-rights.summary: Alaska generally requires covered employers to pay covered employees one and one-half times their regular rate for work beyond eight hours in a day or 40 hours in a workweek, with exemptions and special scheduling rules under the Alaska Wage and Hour Act. Federal overtime law can apply independently, including where an Alaska exemption applies. Coverage depends on the employer, the employee’s actual duties, and any applicable exception; receiving a salary alone does not eliminate overtime rights.

facts.label: State law
facts.value: The Alaska Wage and Hour Act governs state minimum-wage and overtime obligations. Its coverage provisions and exemptions must be read together; not every worker or employer is subject to the same requirements. — AS 23.10.050–23.10.150

facts.label: Daily and weekly triggers
facts.value: For covered employment, overtime is due for hours exceeding eight in a day or 40 in a workweek. The overtime rate is one and one-half times the employee’s regular rate of pay. — AS 23.10.060

facts.label: Small-employer exception
facts.value: Alaska’s overtime requirement does not apply to an employer employing fewer than four employees in the regular course of business. This state exception does not itself remove any separate federal overtime obligation. — AS 23.10.060; 29 U.S.C. § 207

facts.label: Salaried employees
facts.value: Salary payment alone does not establish an exemption. Alaska recognizes exemptions for qualifying bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees, subject to the applicable statutory requirements. A job title alone does not determine exempt status. — AS 23.10.055

The U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division handles complaints under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act. Federal coverage and exemptions are separate from Alaska’s rules.
An employee may bring a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction for unpaid overtime under AS 23.10.110. The statute provides for attorney fees and costs for a prevailing employee.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alaska
bullets: Does Alaska require overtime after eight hours even during a short week? Generally yes for covered, nonexempt employment. Daily overtime is a separate protection from the weekly threshold, although statutory exceptions apply. — AS 23.10.060

Can an employer average a busy week with a quieter week? Generally no. Weekly overtime is determined by the workweek, not by averaging hours across a two-week payroll period. — Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Wage and Hour FAQs

Can an employee recover more than the unpaid wages? AS 23.10.110 provides for an additional equal amount as liquidated damages. A court may reduce or deny liquidated damages when the employer establishes the statutory good-faith defense.

Is there a deadline for a state overtime lawsuit? Alaska provides a two-year limitation for actions seeking unpaid minimum wages, unpaid overtime, or liquidated damages under the state act. Federal claims have separate limitation rules. — AS 23.10.130

employment-law/alaska/wage-theft.summary: In Alaska, wage theft can include unpaid agreed wages, minimum-wage shortfalls, unpaid overtime, and failure to pay final wages on time, subject to the coverage rules and exemptions that apply to the job. Alaska’s minimum wage increased to $14 an hour on July 1, 2026, and covered employees generally earn overtime after eight hours a day or 40 hours a week. Claims may involve the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development or a civil lawsuit.

facts.label: Minimum wage in 2026
facts.value: Alaska’s minimum wage was $13 an hour from January 1 through June 30, 2026, and became $14 an hour on July 1, 2026. Statutory exemptions mean this rate does not cover every worker. — AS 23.10.065; Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Minimum Wage

facts.label: Tips
facts.value: An employer cannot use employee tips as a credit toward Alaska’s required minimum wage. Tips therefore do not replace the employer’s minimum-wage obligation. — AS 23.10.065

facts.label: Overtime
facts.value: Covered employees must receive at least one and one-half times their regular rate for overtime. Alaska generally uses both a daily eight-hour threshold and a weekly 40-hour threshold, subject to statutory exemptions and exceptions. — AS 23.10.060

facts.label: Payroll records
facts.value: Employers must retain required employment records for at least three years, including each employee’s daily and weekly hours and wages paid each pay period. — AS 23.10.100

A court may reduce or deny liquidated damages if the employer establishes statutory good faith and reasonable grounds.
The statute provides for reasonable attorney fees and costs in addition to a judgment for the employee.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alaska
bullets: The Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development’s Wage and Hour Administration receives wage complaints and investigates alleged violations of state wage laws. Its offices serve Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Juneau.

Alaska law authorizes the labor department to take assignments of employee wage claims and pursue collection in qualifying cases. An administrative wage claim and an employee’s lawsuit are distinct enforcement routes. — AS 23.05.220

Alaska courts hear civil claims for unpaid wages. The Alaska Wage and Hour Act expressly permits employees to sue for unpaid statutory minimum wages or overtime and associated remedies. — AS 23.10.110

The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division handles federal Fair Labor Standards Act complaints where federal coverage applies; Alaska’s separate daily-overtime requirement comes from state law.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alaska
bullets: Does receiving a salary automatically eliminate overtime? No. A salary alone does not establish an exemption; Alaska’s statutory exemption requirements still matter. — AS 23.10.055
Can an employee waive Alaska’s minimum-wage or overtime protections? An agreement to work for less than the statutory requirements is not a defense to a recovery action. — AS 23.10.110(a)

Is retaliation for a wage complaint prohibited? Alaska prohibits discharge or other discrimination because an employee filed a complaint or participated in proceedings under the Alaska Wage and Hour Act. — AS 23.10.135

Does the two-year deadline govern every unpaid-wage dispute? The stated two-year period applies to actions under the Alaska Wage and Hour Act. Claims for agreed compensation may involve different legal rules; talk to a lawyer. — AS 23.10.130

employment-law/alaska/workplace-discrimi.summary: Alaska’s Human Rights Law prohibits employment discrimination based on race, religion, color, national origin, age, physical or mental disability, sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, and parenthood. State law generally reaches employers with at least one employee, subject to statutory exclusions, while federal coverage depends on the particular law and employer size. The Alaska State Commission for Human Rights investigates state-law complaints; federal claims generally go through the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

facts.label: Protected employment decisions
facts.value: An employer may not refuse employment, bar someone from employment, or discriminate in compensation or a term, condition, or privilege of employment because of a protected characteristic when the reasonable demands of the position do not require the distinction. The statute contains qualifications concerning age restrictions and pregnancy or parenthood — AS 18.80.220(a)(1).

facts.label: Employer coverage
facts.value: The state definition of employer covers a person employing one or more employees and expressly includes the state and its political subdivisions. It excludes a club that is exclusively social and a corporation, association, or society that is exclusively fraternal, charitable, educational, or religious, if it is not organized and operated for private profit — AS 18.80.300.

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: Alaska prohibits discrimination against someone for opposing practices forbidden by the Human Rights Law or for filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in a proceeding under that law — AS 18.80.220.

facts.label: EEOC charge deadlines
facts.value: The usual federal charge deadline is 180 days. It generally extends to 300 days where a state or local agency enforces a law prohibiting discrimination on the same basis. For age claims, the extension requires applicable state age-discrimination law and a state enforcement authority — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(e)(1); 29 U.S.C. § 626(d).

facts.label: Federal employees
facts.value: Federal employees and applicants generally must contact their employing agency’s EEO counselor within 45 days; this is a separate process from an ordinary private-sector EEOC charge — 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1).

facts.label: State court
facts.value: Alaska superior courts have jurisdiction over civil actions arising under AS 18.80 and may grant relief authorized by the jurisdictional statute, including injunctions — AS 22.10.020(i).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alaska
bullets: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights: the state agency that receives and investigates complaints under the Alaska Human Rights Law — AS 18.80.100–18.80.110.
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: the federal agency handling charges under Title VII, the ADA, and the ADEA.
Alaska Superior Court: the state trial court with jurisdiction over civil actions arising under AS 18.80 — AS 22.10.020(i).

sections.heading: Common questions in Alaska
bullets: Can a small workplace be covered? Yes. Alaska’s employer definition generally starts at one employee, subject to statutory exclusions.
Is parenthood protected? Yes. AS 18.80.220 expressly includes parenthood, with statutory qualifications.
Does federal age protection cover workers under 40? No. The ADEA protects individuals who are at least 40; Alaska separately lists age.
Is retaliation a separate violation? Yes. Alaska expressly prohibits retaliation for protected opposition or participation.

employment-law/arizona/overtime-rights.summary: Arizona does not have a general state overtime law requiring premium pay after eight hours in a day or 40 hours in a week; most overtime rights come from the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). For covered, nonexempt employees, that law generally requires at least one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, while Arizona wage-payment law separately addresses unpaid wages and potential remedies.

sections.heading: Which overtime rules apply in Arizona

facts.label: Federal coverage
facts.value: The FLSA covers employees through enterprise coverage or individual involvement in interstate commerce. Working in Arizona does not, by itself, establish federal coverage. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 203(s), 207(a).

facts.label: Exempt employees
facts.value: Executive, administrative, professional, and outside-sales exemptions depend on the applicable legal requirements, not simply an employer's job title. Receiving a salary alone does not eliminate overtime rights. — 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1); 29 C.F.R. Part 541.

facts.label: Unauthorized work
facts.value: An employer must count work it suffers or permits, including work performed contrary to an advance-approval policy when the employer knows or has reason to know it is being performed. — 29 C.F.R. §§ 785.11–785.13.

facts.label: Arizona wage remedies
facts.value: Arizona defines wages to include nondiscretionary compensation reasonably expected for services. Its wage statute permits a civil claim for treble unpaid wages in qualifying cases; trebling is not automatic for every overtime dispute. — A.R.S. §§ 23-350(7), 23-355(A).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: The U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division, receives and investigates FLSA overtime complaints involving Arizona workplaces. Its national assistance number is 1-866-487-9243.

The Industrial Commission of Arizona's Labor Department administers state wage-payment claims, but does not enforce federal overtime requirements. State wage-payment claims and federal overtime complaints are distinct processes.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona and state courts of competent jurisdiction can hear private FLSA actions. Arizona's unpaid-wage statute also authorizes civil actions. — 29 U.S.C. § 216(b); A.R.S. § 23-355(A).

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Does a 12-hour shift automatically require overtime? No. Arizona has no general daily overtime requirement, and the usual FLSA trigger is more than 40 hours worked in a workweek.
Is weekend or holiday work automatically overtime? No. Federal law does not require premium pay solely because work occurs on a weekend or holiday. — 29 C.F.R. § 778.102.

Can a private employer substitute future time off for overtime pay? Generally not for covered, nonexempt employees. Qualifying public agencies have separate compensatory-time rules. — 29 U.S.C. § 207(o).
Can an employer retaliate over an overtime complaint? The FLSA prohibits retaliation for protected complaints and participation in proceedings. — 29 U.S.C. § 215(a)(3).

employment-law/california/contractor-vs-.summary: California generally uses the ABC test to decide whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under its Labor Code, unemployment insurance law, and wage orders, unless a statutory exception applies. The hiring business must prove all three parts of that test, and a contract or Form 1099 does not settle the issue; misclassification can create liability for unpaid wages, employment taxes, and civil penalties.

facts.label: Default rule
facts.value: A person providing labor or services for payment is presumed to be an employee unless the hiring entity satisfies the ABC test. California Labor Code section 2775 codifies this rule, subject to statutory exceptions. — California Labor Code § 2775(b).

facts.label: Exceptions require separate analysis
facts.value: Specified occupations and business relationships have exceptions with detailed conditions. An exception from the ABC test does not necessarily establish independent-contractor status; many exceptions instead require analysis under the multifactor Borello test. — California Labor Code §§ 2775–2787.

facts.label: Business-to-business arrangements
facts.value: A qualifying business-to-business service relationship may be evaluated under Borello if the contracting business demonstrates that all statutory requirements are satisfied. Forming an LLC or signing a services agreement alone does not establish this exception. — California Labor Code § 2776(a).

rows: The worker is free from the hiring entity’s control and direction in performing the work, both under the contract and in fact.
The work is outside the usual course of the hiring entity’s business.
The worker is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as the work performed.
This multifactor test principally examines the right to control the manner and means of work, together with factors such as a distinct business, tools, skill, and opportunity for profit or loss.
S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations, 48 Cal.3d 341 (1989)

facts.label: Employee protections
facts.value: Misclassified employees may be entitled to unpaid minimum wages, overtime where applicable, and reimbursement of necessary business expenses. Whether particular protections apply depends on the work and any applicable exemptions. — California Labor Code §§ 510, 1194, 2802.

facts.label: Willful-misclassification penalties
facts.value: Willful misclassification carries civil penalties of $5,000–$15,000 per violation. A pattern or practice carries penalties of $10,000–$25,000 per violation. These penalties are additional to other penalties or fines permitted by law. — California Labor Code § 226.8(b)–(c).

facts.label: Meaning of willful
facts.value: For these penalties, willful misclassification means voluntarily and knowingly avoiding employee status by misclassifying an individual as an independent contractor. Not every classification error necessarily meets that definition. — California Labor Code § 226.8(i)(4).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: The California Labor Commissioner’s Office, within the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, handles wage claims and investigates labor-law violations, including alleged misclassification affecting wages.
The Employment Development Department addresses worker classification for California employment-tax purposes and administers unemployment insurance claims.
California superior courts hear civil employment claims, including claims for unpaid wages under Labor Code section 1194. The available forum and remedies depend on the claim.

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Does receiving a Form 1099 make someone a contractor? No. California evaluates the legal test and actual working relationship, not simply the tax form or contract label.
Must the business prove every ABC element? Yes. When the ABC test governs, the hiring entity must establish all three elements to classify the worker as an independent contractor.
Does working remotely establish contractor status? No. Work location alone does not establish the ABC elements or resolve a Borello analysis.
Does an occupational exception eliminate employee rights? No. Many exceptions substitute Borello for the ABC test, and the worker can still qualify as an employee.

employment-law/arizona/wrongful-terminat.summary: Arizona generally permits at-will employment, but a discharge can be unlawful when it breaches a qualifying employment contract, violates an Arizona statute, or retaliates against conduct specifically protected by state law. The Arizona Employment Protection Act defines the principal state wrongful-termination claims and limits some remedies; discrimination claims have a separate administrative process, and Arizona generally imposes a one-year deadline for filing a wrongful-termination lawsuit.

facts.label: At-will employment and contracts
facts.value: Employment is generally terminable by either party. A written contract can restrict termination; a handbook can qualify if it expresses an intent to be an employment contract. The statute also recognizes qualifying writings signed by the party to be charged and preserves collective bargaining agreements. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(2).

facts.label: Statutory limits on claims
facts.value: The Arizona Employment Protection Act identifies claims for breach of a qualifying employment contract, termination violating an Arizona statute, and specified retaliation. When the violated statute provides a remedy, that remedy is exclusive for the statutory-violation claim described in the Act. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)(a)–(b).

facts.label: Protected whistleblowing
facts.value: Protection covers a reasonable disclosure that the employer or an employee has violated, is violating, or will violate the Arizona Constitution or Arizona statutes. The disclosure must go to an employer representative reasonably believed to have investigative and corrective authority, or to an employee of an appropriate public body. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)(c)(ii).

facts.label: Discriminatory discharge
facts.value: The Arizona Civil Rights Act prohibits covered employers from discharging an individual because of race, color, religion, sex, age, national origin, or disability. It also prohibits retaliation for opposing unlawful employment practices or participating in covered proceedings. — A.R.S. § 41-1463(B), (F).

rows: Generally must be commenced within one year after the claim accrues.
An action for breach of an oral or written employment contract generally has a one-year limitation period.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: Arizona Attorney General, Civil Rights Division: receives and investigates employment-discrimination charges under the Arizona Civil Rights Act. The administrative charge process is distinct from filing a court complaint. — A.R.S. § 41-1481.

Arizona Superior Court: hears civil wrongful-termination and employment-contract lawsuits within its jurisdiction. The Arizona Civil Rights Act also authorizes civil enforcement proceedings in superior court. — A.R.S. §§ 23-1501, 41-1481.

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Is an unfair firing automatically illegal? No. Arizona’s at-will rule does not require every discharge to have a fair reason; a claim requires a recognized legal basis. — A.R.S. § 23-1501.
Does every employee handbook create a contract? No. The Act requires the handbook or manual to express an intent that it is a contract of employment. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(2).

Is every workplace complaint protected whistleblowing? No. This provision concerns reasonably believed violations of Arizona constitutional or statutory law and specifies eligible recipients. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)(c)(ii).

Is the discrimination-charge deadline the same as the lawsuit deadline? No. The state discrimination-charge deadline is 180 days, while the general wrongful-termination limitation period is one year. — A.R.S. §§ 41-1481, 12-541.

employment-law/alaska/workplace-harassme.summary: Alaska’s Human Rights Law prohibits employment discrimination based on specified protected characteristics, and workplace harassment can violate that law when it constitutes discriminatory treatment or creates an unlawful hostile work environment. Alaska law can cover employers with as few as one employee, subject to statutory exclusions; federal protections generally have higher employee thresholds. The Alaska State Commission for Human Rights handles state discrimination complaints, while the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission handles claims under federal employment discrimination laws.

facts.label: Protected characteristics
facts.value: Alaska prohibits discrimination in compensation and employment terms, conditions, or privileges because of race, religion, color, national origin, age, physical or mental disability, sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, or parenthood, subject to statutory qualifications and exceptions. Harassment connected to these characteristics can fall within this prohibition. — Alaska Stat. § 18.80.220(a)(1)

facts.label: Employer coverage
facts.value: The state definition of employer includes a person employing one or more employees in Alaska. The definition contains exclusions, including specified nonprofit organizations, so state coverage is not identical to federal coverage. — Alaska Stat. § 18.80.300

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: Alaska prohibits discrimination against a person for opposing practices forbidden by the Human Rights Law or for filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in a proceeding under that law. This is a separate protection from the underlying discrimination prohibition. — Alaska Stat. § 18.80.220(a)(4)

facts.label: Federal harassment standard
facts.value: Under federal law, unlawful harassment includes protected-characteristic-based conduct that becomes a condition of continued employment or is sufficiently severe or pervasive to create an intimidating, hostile, or abusive work environment. Ordinary personality conflicts and isolated incidents generally do not qualify unless extremely serious. — EEOC, Harassment

sections.heading: Federal damages limits for covered employers

columns: Combined compensatory and punitive damages ceiling
rows: Not a ceiling on every remedy
These federal limits cover specified compensatory and punitive damages in intentional Title VII and ADA cases, not back pay; they are not Alaska state-law damages limits.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alaska
bullets: Alaska State Commission for Human Rights: receives and investigates complaints alleging violations of Alaska’s Human Rights Law. Its statutory process includes investigation and efforts to resolve supported complaints through conference, conciliation, and persuasion. — Alaska Stat. §§ 18.80.100–18.80.110

Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: handles federal workplace discrimination and harassment charges. Title VII and the ADA generally cover employers with at least 15 employees; the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act generally requires 20 employees. — 42 U.S.C. §§ 2000e(b), 12111(5); 29 U.S.C. § 630(b)

Alaska Superior Court: state law expressly provides jurisdiction over civil actions arising under the Human Rights Law. An administrative complaint and a civil lawsuit are distinct proceedings. — Alaska Stat. § 22.10.020(i)

sections.heading: Common questions in Alaska
bullets: Is every form of workplace bullying illegal harassment? No. Under discrimination law, the conduct must have the required connection to a protected characteristic and satisfy the applicable legal standard. — Alaska Stat. § 18.80.220; EEOC, Harassment

Can a coworker or customer be the harasser? Yes. Federal harassment law can apply to conduct by supervisors, coworkers, and nonemployees, although employer liability depends on the circumstances. — EEOC, Harassment
Does Alaska protect employees at very small businesses? Potentially yes. The state employer definition starts at one employee, subject to statutory exclusions. — Alaska Stat. § 18.80.300

Is there a deadline after an EEOC right-to-sue notice? Generally, a Title VII or ADA lawsuit must be filed within 90 days after receipt of the notice. That deadline is separate from the deadline for filing an EEOC charge. — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(f)(1); EEOC, Filing a Lawsuit

employment-law/arizona/at-will-employmen.summary: Arizona generally allows either an employer or an employee to end employment at will, but a qualifying written agreement can restrict termination, and specific laws prohibit certain reasons for firing. The Arizona Employment Protection Act limits wrongful-termination claims to recognized categories, including qualifying contract breaches, violations of Arizona statutes, and specified retaliation. Discrimination complaints, wrongful-termination lawsuits, and constructive-discharge claims have different deadlines or procedural requirements; Arizona does not impose a general requirement that employers establish good cause before ending an at-will relationship.

sections.heading: Arizona’s at-will rule and contract exceptions

facts.label: Default employment relationship
facts.value: Employment is a contractual relationship that either side generally may end unless a qualifying written agreement limits termination. The Arizona Employment Protection Act supplies the state’s principal framework for termination claims. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(1)–(3)

facts.label: Written restrictions
facts.value: A written agreement may establish a specified employment duration or otherwise expressly restrict termination. The statute recognizes qualifying signed writings and employment handbooks or similar distributed documents that express an intent to be an employment contract. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(2)

facts.label: Handbooks and verbal promises
facts.value: A handbook does not automatically change at-will status merely because it describes workplace policies. The statute requires contractual intent for the handbook route and states that partial performance does not satisfy its writing requirement. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(2)

rows: Termination may support a claim when it breaches an employment contract meeting the statute’s requirements.
Termination that violates an Arizona statute can support a claim, subject to the statute’s rules about available and exclusive remedies.
The Act protects an employee against termination for refusing to commit an act or omission that would violate the Arizona Constitution or Arizona statutes.
Protection covers qualifying reasonable disclosures of actual or reasonably suspected Arizona constitutional or statutory violations to specified employer representatives or a public-body employee.
Termination in retaliation for exercising rights under Arizona’s workers’ compensation statutes is expressly covered.

facts.label: Wrongful-termination lawsuit
facts.value: Arizona specifies a one-year limitations period for an action for damages for wrongful termination. Different claims can carry different deadlines. — A.R.S. § 12-541(4)

facts.label: State discrimination charge
facts.value: An employment discrimination charge under the Arizona Civil Rights Act must be filed within 180 days after the alleged unlawful employment practice. — A.R.S. § 41-1481(A)

facts.label: Resignation treated as discharge
facts.value: For the objectively intolerable working-conditions route, an employee generally must provide written notice and allow 15 calendar days for the employer’s response before resigning. The statute provides exceptions for outrageous conduct and employer waiver of the notice requirement. — A.R.S. § 23-1502

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: The Arizona Attorney General’s Civil Rights Division receives employment discrimination charges under the Arizona Civil Rights Act. — A.R.S. § 41-1481

Arizona superior courts hear civil employment lawsuits within their jurisdiction, including wrongful-termination claims; the Civil Rights Act also provides for superior-court enforcement actions. — Arizona Constitution, article 6, § 14; A.R.S. § 41-1481

Administrative discrimination proceedings and civil wrongful-termination lawsuits are distinct processes. The Employment Protection Act does not replace a statutory exclusive remedy with a separate claim carrying broader relief. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)(b)

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Must an employer prove good cause? Generally no, unless an applicable contract or law restricts termination. — A.R.S. § 23-1501
Does every unfair firing create a claim? No. Arizona limits termination claims to recognized statutory categories; unfairness alone is not a separate category. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)

Can reporting misconduct be protected? Yes, but the Act’s disclosure protection has requirements concerning the suspected legal violation and the recipient of the report. — A.R.S. § 23-1501(A)(3)(c)(ii)
Can quitting count as being fired? Sometimes. Arizona recognizes constructive discharge, subject to statutory proof and notice rules. — A.R.S. § 23-1502

employment-law/arkansas/unemployment-ben.summary: Arkansas unemployment insurance provides temporary benefits to workers who meet the state’s wage-history and ongoing eligibility requirements; losing a job does not automatically establish eligibility. Under the Arkansas Employment Security Law, claimants generally must be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work, while voluntary quits, misconduct discharges, and refusals of suitable work can cause disqualification. The Arkansas Department of Commerce administers the program, and disputed determinations can proceed through administrative appeals and then judicial review.

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The Arkansas Employment Security Law governs unemployment insurance eligibility, disqualifications, benefit determinations, and appeals. Monetary eligibility and eligibility for a particular week are separate requirements. — Ark. Code Ann. §§ 11-10-101 et seq., 11-10-507.

facts.label: Ability and availability
facts.value: A claimant generally must be physically and mentally able to perform suitable work and available for that work. Statutory exceptions apply to certain claimants and circumstances. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-507.

facts.label: Work search
facts.value: Registration and reporting alone do not establish availability. The law generally requires efforts to secure work that a reasonably prudent person would make, subject to applicable exceptions. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-507.

facts.label: Weekly eligibility
facts.value: Eligibility is evaluated for individual benefit weeks. Arkansas requires continuing claims and information about work, earnings, and other circumstances affecting payment; approval of an initial claim does not guarantee payment for every later week. — Arkansas Division of Workforce Services, Unemployment Insurance.

sections.heading: How the reason for unemployment affects benefits

rows: A layoff does not itself establish a disqualifying quit or misconduct discharge, but wage-history and weekly eligibility requirements still apply.

Leaving work voluntarily without good cause connected with the work generally disqualifies a claimant. The statute contains exceptions, including specified emergencies and health-related circumstances.
Misconduct connected with the work can disqualify a claimant. Being fired and being discharged for statutory misconduct are not automatically the same thing.
Poor performance is not misconduct unless the employer proves intentional conduct; repeated acts despite progressive discipline can establish intentional poor performance.
Failure without good cause to apply for or accept suitable work can cause disqualification. Suitability includes factors such as health, training, experience, prior earnings, and distance.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arkansas
bullets: Initial claims and continuing benefit claims: Arkansas Department of Commerce, Division of Workforce Services unemployment insurance program. Its official unemployment website provides claim-filing access and local office information.

Appeals from agency determinations: Arkansas Appeal Tribunal. An appeal generally must be filed within 20 calendar days after the determination is mailed, or delivered if it is not mailed. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-524.
Further administrative review: Arkansas Board of Review reviews Appeal Tribunal decisions under the Employment Security Law. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-525.
Judicial review: The Arkansas Court of Appeals reviews final Board of Review decisions under the statutory review procedure. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-529.

sections.heading: Common questions in Arkansas
bullets: Can someone receive benefits after quitting? Sometimes. Arkansas recognizes statutory exceptions, but a voluntary quit without good cause connected with the work generally results in disqualification. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-513.

Does an employer decide whether a former employee gets benefits? No. The agency determines eligibility; employers and claimants can challenge determinations through the statutory appeal process. — Ark. Code Ann. §§ 11-10-522 through 11-10-525.
Does every firing count as misconduct? No. Arkansas distinguishes statutory misconduct from discharge alone and specifically addresses when poor performance qualifies. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-514.

Can an appeal be accepted after the deadline? Arkansas permits an appeal to be considered timely when the late filing resulted from circumstances beyond the appellant’s control. — Ark. Code Ann. § 11-10-524.

employment-law/california/unemployment-b.summary: California unemployment insurance provides temporary payments to eligible workers who are unemployed or working reduced hours, have sufficient covered wages, and meet ongoing eligibility requirements administered by the Employment Development Department (EDD). Regular weekly benefits range from $40 to $450, generally for up to 26 weeks, although the amount and duration depend on the claim. Quitting or being fired does not automatically settle eligibility: EDD examines the reason employment ended under California’s unemployment insurance rules.

facts.label: Basic eligibility
facts.value: A claimant generally must have sufficient covered wages, be unemployed, be able and available for work, and seek work as required by EDD. Eligibility is evaluated for individual benefit weeks, not just when the claim begins. — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1253; EDD, Eligibility Requirements.

facts.label: Quitting and discharge
facts.value: A worker may be disqualified for voluntarily leaving the most recent work without good cause or being discharged for misconduct connected with that work. Being fired, by itself, is not the same as a finding of misconduct. — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256.

facts.label: Suitable work
facts.value: Refusing suitable work without good cause can disqualify a claimant. Suitability considers factors including health and safety risks, physical fitness, training, experience, prior earnings, length of unemployment, and distance from available work. — California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1257(b), 1258.

facts.label: Ongoing certification
facts.value: Claimants generally certify for benefits every two weeks. Certification addresses continuing eligibility, including work and earnings during the weeks claimed; an approved claim does not guarantee payment for every subsequent week. — EDD, Eligibility Requirements.

sections.heading: Payment amounts, waiting periods, and deadlines

rows: Regular unemployment insurance pays $40 to $450 per week, depending on covered wages.
Regular benefits are generally available for up to 26 weeks; the claim’s maximum award can limit payment sooner.
A claim generally includes a one-week unpaid waiting period for which eligibility requirements must otherwise be met.
For partial unemployment, the weekly benefit is reduced by wages exceeding $25 or 25% of those wages, whichever exclusion is greater.
An appeal generally must be filed within 30 days after the determination notice is mailed. A late appeal may be accepted for good cause.
California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328; EDD, Appeals

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: EDD administers unemployment insurance claims. Claims may be filed through UI Online, by telephone, or using EDD’s mail or fax procedures.

An appeal from an EDD determination is submitted to the EDD office identified on the notice. If EDD does not resolve the matter favorably, it forwards the appeal for a hearing before an administrative law judge.

The California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board handles unemployment insurance appeals through its administrative hearing system. A further administrative appeal from an administrative law judge’s decision is generally due within 30 days after the decision is mailed. — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334.

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Can someone receive benefits after quitting? Yes, if the separation meets California’s good-cause standard and the other eligibility requirements are satisfied. — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256.
Does an employer decide whether benefits are paid? No. Employers can provide information and appeal determinations, but EDD initially decides eligibility, subject to administrative appeal.
Can reduced hours qualify? Yes. Partial unemployment may qualify, but earnings affect the payment and other eligibility requirements still apply. — Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1252, 1279.
Are unemployment payments taxable? They are generally subject to federal income tax but are not taxable for California personal income tax purposes. — EDD, Tax Information.

employment-law/california/wage-theft.summary: California wage theft can include unpaid minimum wages or overtime, off-the-clock work, unlawful deductions, and withholding earned final pay; many of these protections depend on employee status and applicable exemptions. Employees can pursue wage claims through the California Labor Commissioner’s Office, and state law also authorizes civil lawsuits for unpaid minimum wages and overtime. Depending on the violation, recovery can include unpaid wages, interest, statutory penalties, liquidated damages, and attorney’s fees.

facts.label: Minimum wage and overtime
facts.value: An employee’s agreement to accept less does not eliminate the right to recover unpaid statutory minimum wages or overtime. Labor Code section 1194 authorizes recovery of the unpaid balance, interest, reasonable attorney’s fees, and costs through a civil action. — California Labor Code § 1194

facts.label: Off-the-clock work
facts.value: Under applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, compensable hours include time an employee is subject to employer control and time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required. — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(K)

facts.label: Pay records
facts.value: Employers generally must provide itemized wage statements identifying gross and net wages, deductions, the pay period, and other required information. The requirement to list total hours worked has statutory exceptions. — California Labor Code § 226(a)

rows: For covered nonexempt employees, work beyond eight hours in a workday or 40 hours in a workweek generally earns 1.5 times the regular rate; work beyond 12 hours in a workday generally earns double time.

Failure to provide a legally required meal or rest period generally triggers one additional hour of pay at the regular rate of compensation for the workday. Separate meal and rest violations can support separate premiums.
Earned, unpaid wages generally are due immediately upon discharge, subject to industry-specific exceptions.
For employees without a written contract for a definite period, final wages generally are due within 72 hours after quitting, or at quitting if at least 72 hours’ notice was given.
Willful failure to pay qualifying final wages can produce a penalty calculated at the employee’s daily wage, continuing until payment or commencement of an action, for up to 30 days.
Qualifying minimum-wage claims can include liquidated damages equal to the unpaid minimum wages plus interest. The statute includes a good-faith defense permitting judicial discretion.

facts.label: Wage-claim deadlines
facts.value: The Labor Commissioner identifies a three-year filing period for minimum-wage, overtime, and meal or rest-period claims. Other claims can have different periods, including two years for an oral promise to pay more than minimum wage and four years for a written contract. — California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 337, 338, 339; DLSE wage-claim guidance

facts.label: Protected wage complaints
facts.value: California prohibits retaliation for protected wage complaints, including qualifying internal complaints and Labor Commissioner proceedings. A Labor Commissioner retaliation complaint under section 98.7 generally has a one-year deadline. — California Labor Code §§ 98.6, 98.7

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: California Labor Commissioner’s Office, also called the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement: individual wage claims under Labor Code section 98.
California superior courts: civil actions for unpaid minimum wages or overtime under Labor Code section 1194.
Labor Commissioner’s Retaliation Complaint Investigation Unit: employment-retaliation complaints within its statutory jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Does a salary eliminate overtime rights? No. Exemption depends on the applicable legal requirements, not salary payment alone.
Can an employer keep employee tips? Labor Code section 351 prohibits employers and their agents from taking gratuities left for employees.
Are undocumented workers covered? California Labor Code section 1171.5 generally extends state employment-law protections regardless of immigration status, subject to federal-law limits.
Can employers charge employees necessary business expenses? Labor Code section 2802 generally requires reimbursement of necessary expenditures or losses incurred in performing job duties.

employment-law/colorado/family-medical-l.summary: Colorado provides paid family and medical leave through FAMLI, a state insurance program that generally offers eligible workers up to 12 weeks of benefits, with additional leave available for certain circumstances. Colorado also requires accrued paid sick leave under the Healthy Families and Workplaces Act, while the federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides qualifying employees with unpaid, job-protected leave. These programs have different eligibility, payment, and job-protection rules.

facts.label: Earnings requirement
facts.value: FAMLI eligibility generally requires at least $2,500 in wages subject to premiums during the applicable base period or alternative base period. Benefits replace part of a worker’s wages; they are not necessarily full salary. — C.R.S. §§ 8-13.3-503, 8-13.3-504, 8-13.3-506.

facts.label: Qualifying reasons
facts.value: Covered reasons include the worker’s serious health condition, caring for a family member with a serious health condition, bonding with a new child, qualifying military exigencies, and safe leave related to domestic violence, stalking, sexual assault, or abuse. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-504.

facts.label: Family members
facts.value: Colorado’s definition includes specified relatives and another individual with whom the worker has a significant personal bond that is or is like a family relationship, regardless of biological or legal relationship. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-503.

facts.label: Coverage exceptions
facts.value: Federal employees are outside Colorado FAMLI coverage. Local governments may decline participation, and self-employed individuals may elect coverage. Employers may use approved private plans instead of the state plan. — C.R.S. §§ 8-13.3-503, 8-13.3-514, 8-13.3-515, 8-13.3-522.

rows: Up to 12 weeks per application year for qualifying reasons.
Up to four additional weeks for a serious health condition related to pregnancy complications or childbirth complications.
Beginning in 2026, up to 12 additional weeks while a covered worker’s child receives inpatient care in a neonatal intensive care unit.
Restoration to the same or an equivalent position generally applies after at least 180 days with the current employer before leave begins.
Accrual of at least one hour per 30 hours worked, up to 48 hours per year, unless the employer provides a more generous qualifying policy.
Generally up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave; qualifying military caregiver leave allows up to 26 workweeks.

facts.label: Foreseeable leave
facts.value: FAMLI generally requires at least 30 days’ advance notice to the employer when leave is foreseeable; otherwise, notice is required as soon as practicable. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-505.

facts.label: Overlapping protections
facts.value: FAMLI leave that also qualifies under federal FMLA runs concurrently with FMLA leave. An employer cannot require a worker to exhaust accrued vacation, sick leave, or other paid time off before or while receiving FAMLI benefits. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-510.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment, FAMLI Division: state-plan benefit claims through My FAMLI+ and complaints concerning FAMLI rights.
Colorado Division of Labor Standards and Statistics: Healthy Families and Workplaces Act paid-sick-leave complaints.
U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: federal FMLA complaints.

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Does a small employer automatically escape FAMLI? No. Employer size affects employer premium obligations, not an automatic exclusion of employees from benefits. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-507.
Does federal FMLA cover every worker? No. Eligibility generally requires 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours during the preceding 12 months, and 50 employees within 75 miles. — 29 U.S.C. § 2611.
Can FAMLI be intermittent? Yes. Qualifying leave may be taken intermittently or on a reduced schedule. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-505.
Can an employer retaliate for using FAMLI? No. Colorado prohibits interference with protected rights and retaliation for exercising them. — C.R.S. § 8-13.3-509.

employment-law/colorado/severance-agreem.summary: Colorado generally does not require employers to offer severance pay, but an employment contract or severance plan may create an obligation to provide it. A severance agreement cannot replace payment of earned wages, and its confidentiality, release, and restrictive-covenant terms are subject to separate state and federal limits. Colorado specifically regulates agreements restricting disclosure of alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practices, while federal law imposes additional safeguards for waivers of age-discrimination claims by employees age 40 or older.

sections.heading: Severance pay and earned wages in Colorado

facts.label: Severance is separate from statutory wages
facts.value: The Colorado Wage Act expressly excludes severance pay from its definition of wages or compensation. Whether severance is owed can instead depend on an agreement or applicable benefit plan. — C.R.S. § 8-4-101(14).

facts.label: Earned compensation remains payable
facts.value: An employer's obligations to pay earned wages when employment ends are governed by the Wage Act, not merely by the severance offer. Agreements waiving or modifying an employee's rights in violation of the Act are void. — C.R.S. §§ 8-4-109, 8-4-121.

facts.label: Vacation pay
facts.value: Earned and determinable vacation pay owed under an employer's vacation policy must be paid upon separation; a severance release does not eliminate statutory wage protections. — C.R.S. §§ 8-4-101(14)(a)(III), 8-4-121.

sections.heading: Limits on confidentiality and restrictive covenants

facts.label: Discrimination-related nondisclosure
facts.value: Colorado's Protecting Opportunities and Workers' Rights Act restricts provisions limiting disclosure of alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practices. Enforceability requires specified safeguards, including equal application to all parties, permitted disclosures, and an addendum signed by all parties attesting to compliance. — C.R.S. § 24-34-407.

facts.label: Protected disclosures
facts.value: A covered nondisclosure provision cannot prohibit disclosures to specified people, including an employee's attorney, or to government agencies for any reason. The statute also protects disclosures made in response to legal process and other legally required disclosures. — C.R.S. § 24-34-407.

facts.label: Noncompete clauses
facts.value: Including a noncompete in a severance agreement does not exempt it from Colorado's restrictive-covenant law. Enforceability depends on statutory exceptions and requirements, including compensation, trade-secret protection, scope, and notice where applicable. — C.R.S. § 8-2-113.

rows: Federal waiver safeguards apply to employees age 40 or older. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 631(a), 626(f).
At least 21 days to consider an individual termination waiver. — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(F).
At least 45 days for an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class. — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(F).
At least seven days after signing to revoke; the waiver is not effective until that period expires. — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(G).
The waiver must specifically identify ADEA rights, provide additional consideration, and advise consultation with an attorney in writing. Future claims cannot be waived. — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment, Division of Labor Standards and Statistics: earned-wage complaints under the Colorado Wage Act; severance itself is excluded from statutory wages.

Colorado Civil Rights Division: employment-discrimination charges under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act. The state filing deadline is generally 300 days after the alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practice. — C.R.S. § 24-34-403.

U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: federal employment-discrimination charges. A release cannot prevent filing an EEOC charge or participating in an EEOC proceeding. — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(4).

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Is severance automatically required after a layoff? No. Colorado does not generally mandate severance pay.
Does every employee receive 21 days to review? No. That federal minimum concerns qualifying ADEA waivers, not every severance agreement.
Can confidentiality cover discrimination allegations? Only if the provision satisfies Colorado's statutory requirements.
Can a release waive future age-discrimination claims? No. The ADEA prohibits waiving claims arising after execution.

employment-law/colorado/workplace-harass.summary: Colorado prohibits workplace harassment under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA), and its Protecting Opportunities and Workers’ Rights (POWR) Act expressly rejects a requirement that harassment be severe or pervasive. Harassment must involve unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic and satisfy statutory subjective and objective offensiveness standards. Colorado’s protections generally reach employers too small for federal Title VII coverage, and state employment discrimination charges ordinarily must be filed with the Colorado Civil Rights Division within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory practice.

facts.label: What qualifies
facts.value: Harassment includes unwelcome physical or verbal conduct, or written, pictorial, or visual communication, directed at someone because of membership or perceived membership in a protected class. It must be subjectively offensive to the person alleging harassment and objectively offensive to a reasonable member of the same protected class. Additional statutory conditions connect the conduct to employment or the work environment. — C.R.S. § 24-34-402.

facts.label: Severity and context
facts.value: Conduct need not be severe or pervasive. Petty slights, minor annoyances, and lack of good manners ordinarily do not qualify unless, individually or together, they meet the statutory standard. The totality of the circumstances matters. — C.R.S. § 24-34-402.

facts.label: Protected characteristics
facts.value: CADA’s employment protections include disability, race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, religion, age, national origin, and ancestry. Race includes hair texture, hair type, and protective hairstyles commonly or historically associated with race. — C.R.S. §§ 24-34-301, 24-34-402.

sections.heading: Coverage, filing periods, and court deadlines

columns: Colorado rule or applicable federal rule
rows: CADA generally covers employers without Title VII’s 15-employee minimum; statutory exclusions apply.
Generally 300 days after the alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practice.
For Title VII harassment claims in Colorado, the filing period generally extends to 300 days.
A CADA civil action generally must begin within 90 days after receipt of the applicable notice of right to sue.
A Title VII lawsuit generally must begin within 90 days after receipt of the EEOC right-to-sue notice.

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: Colorado prohibits retaliation for opposing a discriminatory practice or participating in proceedings under CADA, including making a charge, testifying, or assisting an investigation. A retaliation claim is distinct from the underlying harassment claim. — C.R.S. § 24-34-402.

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: Available relief can include reinstatement, back pay, front pay, injunctive relief, and attorney fees. Compensatory and punitive damages are available for qualifying intentional discrimination claims, subject to statutory restrictions and limits; punitive damages are unavailable against government defendants. — C.R.S. §§ 24-34-405, 24-34-306.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: The Colorado Civil Rights Division receives and investigates employment discrimination charges under CADA. The Colorado Civil Rights Commission has administrative enforcement responsibilities. — C.R.S. § 24-34-306.
The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission handles federal employment discrimination charges, including Title VII harassment and retaliation claims.

Colorado district courts hear CADA civil actions following applicable administrative requirements. The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado hears federal employment discrimination lawsuits within its jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Must harassment be severe or pervasive? No. Colorado expressly removes that requirement, but the other statutory elements still apply.
Does every rude workplace interaction violate CADA? No. Harassment must have the required connection to a protected characteristic and meet Colorado’s statutory standard.
Can one incident qualify? Potentially. Colorado evaluates the totality of the circumstances rather than imposing a minimum number of incidents.
Does an internal complaint replace an agency charge? No. An employer’s internal process is separate from the administrative charge process and generally does not extend filing deadlines.

Colorado Civil Rights Division

employment-law/colorado/overtime-rights.summary: Colorado generally requires overtime pay for covered, nonexempt employees who work more than 40 hours in a workweek, 12 hours in a workday, or 12 consecutive hours, even when those consecutive hours cross midnight. The Colorado Overtime and Minimum Pay Standards Order requires at least one and one-half times the employee’s regular rate, although exemptions and occupation-specific rules can change coverage. Unpaid overtime may be pursued through the Colorado Division of Labor Standards and Statistics or a court.

facts.label: State overtime rule
facts.value: The Colorado Overtime and Minimum Pay Standards Order, commonly called COMPS, establishes overtime requirements for covered employment. Its general thresholds include both weekly and daily overtime, unlike the federal law’s general weekly-only standard. — 7 CCR 1103-1, Rule 4; 29 U.S.C. § 207(a).

facts.label: Regular rate
facts.value: Overtime is based on the regular rate, which is not necessarily the employee’s stated hourly wage. Certain bonuses, commissions, and other compensation must be included; legally excludable payments are treated differently. — 7 CCR 1103-1, Rule 1, definition of regular rate of pay; 29 U.S.C. § 207(e).

facts.label: Salary and exemptions
facts.value: A salary alone does not eliminate overtime rights. Colorado’s executive or supervisor, administrative, and professional exemptions have specific requirements, including applicable duties and compensation tests. Agricultural employment has separate overtime provisions rather than the ordinary daily and weekly framework. — 7 CCR 1103-1, Rules 2 and 4.

sections.heading: When overtime and paid time apply

rows: More than 40 hours in a workweek
Covered, nonexempt employees generally earn overtime for hours above 40; hours cannot be averaged across multiple workweeks.
More than 12 hours in a workday
The general daily overtime threshold applies even when weekly hours remain below 40.
The general consecutive-hours threshold applies regardless of when the workday begins and ends, excluding duty-free meal periods.
The calculation producing the greater payment controls; the same hours do not generate duplicate overtime premiums.
Required rest periods count as time worked when determining overtime eligibility.

facts.label: Limitations period
facts.value: Colorado wage-law actions generally have a two-year limitations period, extended to three years for willful violations. Federal unpaid-overtime actions also generally use two years, or three years for willful violations. — C.R.S. § 8-4-122; 29 U.S.C. § 255(a).

facts.label: Additional recovery
facts.value: Colorado law provides penalties for qualifying failures to pay wages after the statutory demand or notice process. Federal law permits unpaid overtime plus an equal amount as liquidated damages, subject to statutory defenses. — C.R.S. § 8-4-109; 29 U.S.C. §§ 216(b), 260.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: The Colorado Department of Labor and Employment’s Division of Labor Standards and Statistics administers the state wage complaint process and enforces COMPS.
The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division handles complaints involving federal Fair Labor Standards Act overtime requirements.
Colorado courts hear state unpaid-wage claims; federal FLSA claims may be brought in a court with jurisdiction. — C.R.S. § 8-4-110; 29 U.S.C. § 216(b).

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Does working Saturday automatically mean overtime? No. The applicable hours thresholds, rather than the day’s name, generally determine overtime.
Can a salaried employee receive overtime? Yes. Salaried employees who do not qualify for an exemption can remain entitled to overtime.
Does unauthorized overtime have to be paid? Work an employer suffers or permits must be counted; a preapproval policy does not erase payment obligations. — 7 CCR 1103-1, Rule 1.
Can an employer retaliate over a wage complaint? Colorado law prohibits retaliation for protected wage complaints and related activity. — C.R.S. § 8-4-120.

employment-law/colorado/wrongful-termina.summary: Colorado generally follows at-will employment, so a discharge is not automatically unlawful merely because it is unfair or unexplained; however, employers cannot terminate workers for reasons prohibited by discrimination, retaliation, leave, or other employment laws. Wrongful termination can also involve a violated employment agreement or Colorado’s public-policy exception, and the available claim, filing deadline, forum, and remedy depend on the legal basis for challenging the discharge.

sections.heading: When termination can be unlawful in Colorado

facts.label: At-will employment and public policy
facts.value: Colorado recognizes a wrongful-discharge claim when termination violates a clear mandate of public policy. This exception can cover discharge for refusing to perform an illegal act or for exercising an important job-related right; it does not make every unfair firing actionable. — Martin Marietta Corp. v. Lorenz, 823 P.2d 100 (Colo. 1992)

facts.label: Employment promises
facts.value: An employee handbook or employer promise can sometimes support an implied-contract or promissory-estoppel claim. Whether a promise limits the employer’s right to discharge depends on its language and the surrounding circumstances. — Continental Air Lines, Inc. v. Keenan, 731 P.2d 708 (Colo. 1987)

facts.label: Discrimination and retaliation
facts.value: The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discriminatory discharge and retaliation for opposing prohibited discrimination or participating in protected proceedings. Colorado’s employment-discrimination protections generally reach employers with one or more employees, subject to statutory exclusions. — C.R.S. §§ 24-34-401, 24-34-402

rows: Discharge because of protected characteristics, including disability, race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, religion, age, national origin, or ancestry.
Retaliation for filing a wage complaint, participating in wage proceedings, or otherwise exercising rights protected by the Colorado Wage Act.
Retaliation for exercising rights under the Healthy Families and Workplaces Act, including requesting or using protected sick leave.
Interference with protected FAMLI rights and retaliation for exercising those rights.
Termination because of lawful activity away from the employer’s premises during nonworking hours, subject to statutory occupational and conflict-of-interest exceptions.

facts.label: Colorado discrimination charge
facts.value: A charge generally must be filed with the Colorado Civil Rights Division within 300 days after the alleged discriminatory or unfair employment practice. Administrative filing requirements differ from deadlines for filing a lawsuit. — C.R.S. § 24-34-306(1)

facts.label: Federal discrimination charge
facts.value: In Colorado, the EEOC charge deadline is generally 300 days for covered employment-discrimination claims. Federal coverage requirements and exceptions still apply. — EEOC, Time Limits for Filing a Charge

facts.label: Final earned wages
facts.value: When an employer discharges an employee, earned, vested, determinable, and unpaid compensation is generally due immediately. The statute provides exceptions involving an accounting unit’s operating hours or off-site location. — C.R.S. § 8-4-109(1)(a)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: Colorado Civil Rights Division: investigates employment-discrimination and retaliation charges under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act.
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: handles charges under federal employment-discrimination laws.

Colorado Department of Labor and Employment, Division of Labor Standards and Statistics: handles wage and Healthy Families and Workplaces Act complaints; its FAMLI Division administers family and medical leave insurance.
Colorado state courts: hear contract and common-law wrongful-discharge claims. Federal courts hear qualifying federal employment lawsuits, subject to jurisdictional and administrative prerequisites.

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Is an unfair firing necessarily illegal? No. At-will employment permits many terminations that are unfair but do not violate a statute, enforceable promise, or public policy.
Does a small employer escape Colorado discrimination law? Not necessarily. CADA generally covers employers with one or more employees, although statutory exclusions apply.

Does lawful off-duty activity include all marijuana use? No. Colorado’s Supreme Court held that activity unlawful under federal law is not protected by this statute. — Coats v. Dish Network, LLC, 2015 CO 44.
Can different claims have different deadlines? Yes. Discrimination charges, wage claims, contract claims, and public-policy claims do not share one universal deadline. Talk to a lawyer.

employment-law/connecticut/workplace-har.summary: Connecticut prohibits workplace harassment based on protected characteristics under the Connecticut Fair Employment Practices Act, which generally covers employers with at least one employee. Sexual harassment is expressly prohibited, and retaliation for opposing discriminatory practices or participating in discrimination proceedings is also unlawful. Employment discrimination complaints ordinarily must reach the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory act; federal law provides a separate enforcement route for covered employers.

facts.label: State law and employer coverage
facts.value: The Connecticut Fair Employment Practices Act generally defines an employer as a person employing one or more employees, including the state and its political subdivisions. This makes state coverage broader than the usual federal Title VII threshold of 15 employees. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 46a-51(10), 46a-60; 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b)

facts.label: Protected characteristics
facts.value: Connecticut employment law protects characteristics including race, color, religious creed, age, sex, gender identity or expression, marital status, national origin, ancestry, qualifying veteran status, sexual orientation, and specified mental, intellectual, learning, and physical disabilities. Harassment must have a legally prohibited basis; ordinary workplace incivility alone is not necessarily discrimination. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 46a-60(b)(1), 46a-81c

facts.label: Sexual harassment
facts.value: The statute covers unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other sexual conduct when submission becomes an employment condition, submission or rejection affects employment decisions, or the conduct substantially interferes with work or creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46a-60(b)(8)

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: Discharging, expelling, or otherwise discriminating against someone for opposing a discriminatory employment practice, filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in a covered proceeding is prohibited. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46a-60(b)(4)

rows: Generally due within 300 days after the alleged discriminatory act for employment practices occurring on or after October 1, 2019.
An action following a release must be brought within 90 days after receipt; separate statutory timing requirements also apply.
Employers must provide employees with two hours of sexual harassment education and training; new employees generally must receive it within six months of hiring.
Employers with fewer than three employees must train supervisory employees; new supervisors generally must receive training within six months of assuming supervisory duties.
Employers must provide supplemental training at least every ten years.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Connecticut
bullets: The Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO) receives and investigates state employment discrimination and harassment complaints through its regional offices. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 46a-82, 46a-83.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) handles federal workplace discrimination complaints. In Connecticut, Title VII charges generally have a 300-day filing period; federal employee procedures differ. — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(e).

Connecticut Superior Court hears authorized civil actions after the CHRO release process. Available court relief includes appropriate legal and equitable relief, attorney fees, and court costs. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 46a-100–46a-104.

sections.heading: Common questions in Connecticut
bullets: Does Connecticut law cover a two-person employer? Yes. The state-law employer definition generally reaches employers with one or more employees. — § 46a-51(10).
Must harassment involve sexual conduct? No. Harassment based on other protected characteristics can constitute unlawful employment discrimination. — §§ 46a-60, 46a-81c.
Can an employer punish someone for supporting a complaint? Retaliation for protected opposition or participation is prohibited. — § 46a-60(b)(4).
Does completing training eliminate liability? No. Training requirements and the prohibition against discriminatory employment practices are separate statutory obligations. — §§ 46a-54, 46a-60.
