employment-law/connecticut/overtime-righ.summary: Connecticut generally requires employers to pay covered employees at least one and one-half times their regular hourly rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, under Connecticut General Statutes § 31-76c. Coverage depends on statutory exemptions and the employee’s actual work, not simply whether the employer pays a salary or uses a managerial title. Unpaid overtime may be pursued through the Connecticut Department of Labor or a civil lawsuit, and state law can allow enhanced damages and attorney’s fees.

facts.label: Basic entitlement
facts.value: A covered employee must receive at least one and one-half times the regular rate for employment beyond 40 hours in a workweek. Connecticut’s general overtime rule uses a weekly threshold rather than a daily threshold. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-76c

facts.label: Regular rate
facts.value: The regular rate generally includes remuneration for employment, subject to statutory exclusions. Certain gifts, expense reimbursements, qualifying discretionary bonuses, and other specified payments may be excluded; the base hourly wage is not necessarily the entire regular rate. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-76b

facts.label: Hours worked
facts.value: Hours worked include time an employee is required to be on the employer’s premises, on duty, or at the prescribed workplace, and time the employee is employed or permitted to work. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-76b

facts.label: Exemptions
facts.value: Connecticut exempts specified categories from its overtime requirements, including employees working in bona fide executive, administrative, or professional capacities as defined by applicable law. Salary payment alone does not establish that an employee fits one of these exemptions. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-76i

sections.heading: How the weekly overtime rule applies

rows: Covered hours above 40 receive at least 1.5 times the regular rate.
The general statute does not require overtime solely because a shift exceeds eight hours.
The day itself does not trigger overtime under the general weekly rule.
The statutory threshold applies by workweek, not by averaging hours across the payroll period.
Overtime may still be required unless a statutory exemption applies.

facts.label: Civil filing period
facts.value: Connecticut generally imposes a two-year limitation on actions for remuneration payable periodically, measured from when the right of action accrues. Section 52-596 also contains a tolling provision for qualifying complaints filed with the Labor Commissioner. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-596

facts.label: Unpaid overtime recovery
facts.value: Section 31-68 authorizes recovery of twice the unpaid overtime amount, plus costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. If the employer establishes the statutory good-faith defense, recovery is limited to the unpaid amount plus costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-68

facts.label: Protected complaints
facts.value: Connecticut prohibits discharge or other discrimination because an employee makes a covered wage complaint, institutes a proceeding, or testifies or is about to testify in such a proceeding. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 31-69

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Connecticut
bullets: Connecticut Department of Labor, Wage and Workplace Standards Division: administers state wage-and-hour requirements and accepts complaints involving unpaid wages, including overtime.
Connecticut Superior Court: civil actions under § 31-68 may seek unpaid overtime and the additional recovery authorized by that section.

sections.heading: Common questions in Connecticut
bullets: Does a salary eliminate overtime rights? No. The applicable exemption requirements still matter (§ 31-76i).
Is overtime automatic after eight hours in one day? No. Connecticut’s general rule requires more than 40 hours in a workweek (§ 31-76c).
Does Sunday work automatically earn time-and-a-half? No. Sunday alone does not trigger the general statutory overtime premium (§ 31-76c).
Can an employer retaliate over an overtime complaint? Connecticut law prohibits retaliation for covered complaints and proceedings (§ 31-69).

employment-law/delaware/workplace-discri.summary: Delaware’s Discrimination in Employment Act generally covers employers with four or more employees in Delaware and prohibits discrimination in hiring, discharge, compensation, and other employment terms based on specified protected characteristics. The Delaware Department of Labor handles state employment discrimination charges, while the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforces overlapping federal laws; coverage and procedures differ, and Delaware generally requires an administrative charge before a state discrimination lawsuit.

facts.label: State employer coverage
facts.value: The Delaware Discrimination in Employment Act generally defines an employer as a person employing four or more employees within Delaware at the time of the alleged violation. Its definition includes state and local government employers. — 19 Del. C. § 710.

facts.label: Protected characteristics
facts.value: Protected characteristics include race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, age, genetic information, and reproductive health decisions. The statute also protects specified victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses, or stalking. Statutory definitions and exceptions apply. — 19 Del. C. §§ 710–711.

facts.label: Pregnancy and disability
facts.value: Delaware requires reasonable accommodations for known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth, or related conditions, subject to statutory requirements and an undue-hardship defense. Disability discrimination and reasonable accommodation are also addressed separately in the Persons With Disabilities Employment Protections Act. — 19 Del. C. § 711; §§ 720–728.

sections.heading: Conduct covered by Delaware employment discrimination law

rows: An employer cannot refuse to hire or discharge someone because of a protected characteristic.
Discrimination in compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment is prohibited.
Discriminatory employee classifications that deprive people of employment opportunities or adversely affect employment status are prohibited.
Protection extends to opposing unlawful discrimination and participating in a discrimination investigation, proceeding, or hearing.
Delaware expressly addresses sexual harassment, including circumstances establishing employer responsibility for supervisory or coworker harassment.

facts.label: State charge deadline
facts.value: A Delaware employment discrimination charge generally must be filed with the Department of Labor within 300 days of the alleged unlawful employment practice. — 19 Del. C. § 712.

facts.label: State lawsuit process
facts.value: A state-law civil action requires exhaustion of the administrative remedies established by the chapter. Delaware’s enforcement provisions address investigation, conciliation, right-to-sue notices, and civil litigation. — 19 Del. C. §§ 712–714.

facts.label: Federal timing is separate
facts.value: EEOC charges generally have a 180-day deadline, extended to 300 days when a qualifying state or local agency enforces a law prohibiting discrimination on the same basis. Federal employees generally face a different administrative process. — EEOC, Time Limits for Filing a Charge.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Delaware
bullets: Delaware Department of Labor, Division of Industrial Affairs: administers the state employment discrimination complaint process.
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: receives charges under federal employment discrimination laws.
Delaware Superior Court: hears civil actions authorized by Delaware’s employment discrimination statute after applicable administrative requirements. — 19 Del. C. § 714.
U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware: hears federal employment discrimination lawsuits within its jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Common questions in Delaware
bullets: Can a small employer be covered? Yes. Delaware’s general discrimination law reaches employers with four or more employees within Delaware.
Is every unfair workplace decision illegal discrimination? No. The discrimination prohibition concerns protected characteristics; retaliation and other statutory protections provide separate grounds.
Are applicants protected? Yes. The prohibition against discriminatory refusal to hire protects applicants.
Can complaining trigger lawful retaliation? No. Opposition to unlawful discrimination and participation in covered proceedings are protected activities.

employment-law/florida/workplace-harassm.summary: Florida’s Civil Rights Act prohibits employment discrimination that includes harassment because of race, color, religion, sex, pregnancy, national origin, age, handicap, or marital status, and it prohibits retaliation for opposing unlawful discrimination or participating in proceedings under the Act. For covered employers, actionable harassment generally means discriminatory conduct that changes employment conditions through a tangible employment action or a hostile work environment; a Florida Commission on Human Relations complaint generally must be filed within 365 days of the alleged violation.

facts.label: Covered employers
facts.value: The Florida Civil Rights Act generally covers employers with at least 15 employees for each working day in at least 20 calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Its employer definition includes an employer’s agents. — Fla. Stat. § 760.02(7)

facts.label: Protected characteristics
facts.value: Florida prohibits discrimination in compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, pregnancy, national origin, age, handicap, or marital status. The statute uses the term “handicap.” — Fla. Stat. § 760.10(1)(a)

facts.label: Harassment threshold
facts.value: Under federal employment discrimination law, offensive conduct can become unlawful when enduring it is a condition of continued employment or when it is severe or pervasive enough to create an objectively hostile or abusive workplace. Ordinary annoyances and isolated incidents generally do not qualify unless extremely serious. — EEOC, Harassment

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: Florida separately prohibits discrimination against someone for opposing an unlawful employment practice or making a charge, testifying, assisting, or participating in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under the Act. — Fla. Stat. § 760.10(7)

rows: A complaint may be filed with the Florida Commission on Human Relations within 365 days of the alleged violation.
The commission has 180 days after filing to determine whether reasonable cause exists.
A civil action generally must begin within one year after the commission’s reasonable-cause determination.
An administrative hearing may be requested within 35 days of the determination; failure to request it bars the claim under the Act.
Punitive damages under the Act cannot exceed $100,000 and are unavailable against the state or its agencies or subdivisions.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Florida
bullets: Florida Commission on Human Relations: The state agency receives employment discrimination complaints under the Florida Civil Rights Act and investigates whether reasonable cause exists. — Fla. Stat. § 760.11(1)–(3)

U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: The EEOC handles harassment charges under federal employment discrimination laws. Federal coverage and remedies are distinct from Florida’s statutory provisions. — EEOC, Harassment

Florida courts: Following the required administrative process, the Act authorizes a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction. Available relief includes injunctions, back pay, compensatory damages, and potentially attorney’s fees. — Fla. Stat. § 760.11(4)–(5)
Administrative hearings: The commission or an administrative law judge may hear an administrative claim; this route is distinct from a civil lawsuit. — Fla. Stat. § 760.11(6)–(7)

sections.heading: Common questions in Florida
bullets: Is every instance of workplace bullying illegal harassment? No. A hostile-work-environment discrimination claim requires a connection to a legally protected characteristic and sufficiently serious conduct; ordinary workplace friction is not automatically unlawful. — EEOC, Harassment

Can a customer or coworker be the harasser? Yes. Federal harassment law recognizes harassment by coworkers and nonemployees, as well as supervisors; employer liability depends on the circumstances. — EEOC, Harassment

Does Florida protect employees who report discrimination? Yes. Opposition to unlawful discrimination and participation in proceedings under the Act are protected from retaliation. — Fla. Stat. § 760.10(7)

What if the commission makes no determination within 180 days? The complainant may proceed under the Act as though reasonable cause had been found; additional procedural and timing requirements still apply. — Fla. Stat. § 760.11(8)

employment-law/georgia/overtime-rights.summary: Georgia does not have a general state overtime law, so overtime rights for most covered employees come from the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). Covered, nonexempt employees generally must receive at least one and one-half times their regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek, rather than for simply working a long day, weekend, or holiday. Coverage, exemptions, and what counts as working time determine whether overtime is owed.

sections.heading: Which overtime rules apply in Georgia

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: Georgia has no general state overtime requirement. The federal FLSA supplies the principal overtime rule for covered, nonexempt employees — 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1); Georgia Department of Labor, Laws and Rules.

facts.label: Federal coverage
facts.value: Coverage can arise through an employee's own interstate-commerce work or employment by a covered enterprise. The enterprise definition generally includes businesses with at least $500,000 in annual gross sales or business done and separately covers certain hospitals, schools, and public agencies — 29 U.S.C. §§ 203(s), 207(a).

facts.label: Exempt employees
facts.value: The FLSA exempts qualifying executive, administrative, professional, and outside-sales employees from overtime. A job title or salary alone does not establish an exemption; the applicable regulatory requirements must be met — 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1); 29 C.F.R. Part 541.

rows: Overtime generally starts after 40 hours actually worked in a workweek.
A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours; hours cannot ordinarily be averaged across two or more weeks.
Generally includes remuneration for employment, subject to statutory exclusions; it is not necessarily just the stated hourly rate.
Working more than eight hours in a day, or working weekends or holidays, does not by itself trigger the general federal overtime requirement.
Work an employer suffers or permits counts even when not requested. A rule against unauthorized overtime does not erase compensable hours.
Paid vacation, holiday, or sick time when no work occurs generally does not count toward the 40-hour threshold.

facts.label: Limitations period
facts.value: An FLSA unpaid-overtime action generally has a two-year limitations period, extended to three years for a willful violation — 29 U.S.C. § 255(a).

facts.label: Available recovery
facts.value: Employees may recover unpaid overtime and an equal amount as liquidated damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs. A court may reduce or deny liquidated damages if the employer proves statutory good faith and reasonable grounds — 29 U.S.C. § 216(b); 29 U.S.C. § 260.

facts.label: Retaliation
facts.value: The FLSA prohibits discharge or discrimination for protected complaints or participation in covered proceedings. Remedies can include reinstatement, lost wages, and liquidated damages — 29 U.S.C. §§ 215(a)(3), 216(b).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: The U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division investigates federal overtime complaints involving Georgia employment. Its national assistance number is 1-866-487-9243.
The Georgia Department of Labor does not enforce the FLSA's overtime requirements; its Laws and Rules page identifies federal wage-and-hour law as U.S. Department of Labor jurisdiction.
Private FLSA actions may be brought in a federal or state court of competent jurisdiction. Georgia has Northern, Middle, and Southern federal judicial districts — 29 U.S.C. § 216(b); 28 U.S.C. § 90.

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Does receiving a salary eliminate overtime rights? No. Salaried employees can remain nonexempt — 29 C.F.R. Part 541.

Can a private employer substitute future time off for required overtime pay? Generally no. The statutory compensatory-time exception applies to qualifying state and local public employment — 29 U.S.C. § 207(o).
Can an employer average a 50-hour week with a 30-hour week? Generally no. Each workweek stands alone — 29 C.F.R. § 778.104.
Are short breaks compensable? Rest breaks lasting about five to 20 minutes generally count as working time — 29 C.F.R. § 785.18.

employment-law/idaho/non-compete-agreeme.summary: Idaho permits employment noncompete agreements for key employees and key independent contractors when the restrictions protect legitimate business interests and are reasonable in duration, geographic reach, and the work restricted. Idaho Code Title 44, Chapter 27 establishes rebuttable presumptions for certain restrictions, including an eighteen-month duration, but does not make every noncompete enforceable. Courts can limit or modify unreasonable provisions, and enforceability depends on the agreement, the worker’s role, and the employer’s actual business interests.

sections.heading: Which workers and interests Idaho law covers

facts.label: Covered workers
facts.value: The statute authorizes written restrictive agreements involving key employees and key independent contractors. Its definition focuses on workers whose employer-provided knowledge, influence, reputation, or relationships give them the ability to threaten the employer’s legitimate business interests. It does not treat every worker as a key employee simply because the worker signed an agreement. — Idaho Code §§ 44-2701–44-2702.

facts.label: Protected business interests
facts.value: Legitimate business interests include goodwill, technologies, intellectual property, business plans, business processes and methods, customer and vendor relationships, referral sources, financial and marketing information, and trade secrets. The statutory list is nonexclusive. — Idaho Code § 44-2702.

facts.label: Basic enforceability standard
facts.value: Restrictions must be reasonable in duration, geographical area, and type of employment or line of business. They must not impose a greater restraint than reasonably necessary to protect the employer’s legitimate business interests. — Idaho Code § 44-2701.

rows: A restriction lasting eighteen months or less is rebuttably presumed reasonable.
A restriction limited to areas where the worker provided services or had a significant presence or influence is rebuttably presumed reasonable.
A restriction limited to the type of employment or line of business the worker conducted during the two years before termination is rebuttably presumed reasonable.
A worker among the employer’s highest-paid five percent of employees or independent contractors is rebuttably presumed to be a key employee or key independent contractor.

facts.label: Modification rather than automatic invalidation
facts.value: When an agreement is unreasonable in a respect covered by the statute, the court must limit or modify it as necessary to reflect the parties’ intent and render it reasonable in light of the circumstances in which it was made. — Idaho Code § 44-2703.

facts.label: Presumptions are not guarantees
facts.value: The statutory presumptions are rebuttable. An eighteen-month restriction is therefore not automatically enforceable, and the compensation presumption does not conclusively establish key-worker status. The statute also permits restrictions exceeding eighteen months when additional consideration is specifically given for extending the restriction beyond that period. — Idaho Code §§ 44-2701, 44-2704.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Idaho
bullets: Idaho district courts hear civil disputes involving enforcement of employment noncompetes, including requests for injunctive relief. District courts have original jurisdiction in civil cases. — Idaho Constitution, Article V, § 20.

Title 44, Chapter 27 addresses judicial enforcement; it does not establish a separate administrative complaint process or agency tribunal for deciding whether an employment noncompete is enforceable. — Idaho Code §§ 44-2701–44-2704.

sections.heading: Common questions in Idaho
bullets: Are employment noncompetes banned? No. Idaho expressly permits qualifying written agreements for key employees and key independent contractors, subject to reasonableness requirements. — Idaho Code § 44-2701.
Can an independent contractor be covered? Yes. The statute expressly includes key independent contractors. — Idaho Code §§ 44-2701–44-2702.
Does an overbroad restriction necessarily disappear? No. Idaho directs courts to limit or modify unreasonable agreements under the statutory standard. — Idaho Code § 44-2703.
Does being highly paid automatically make a worker key? No. The highest-paid-five-percent rule creates a rebuttable presumption, not a conclusive classification. — Idaho Code § 44-2704.

employment-law/illinois/at-will-employme.summary: Illinois generally follows at-will employment: absent an enforceable agreement or legal protection, an employer may end employment without proving good cause, and an employee may leave without giving a reason. At-will status does not permit discrimination, retaliation, or discharge that violates clearly mandated public policy, and Illinois statutes protect certain reports of wrongdoing, workplace rights, and earned compensation even when the termination itself is otherwise lawful.

sections.heading: Illinois’s at-will rule and its limits

facts.label: Default rule
facts.value: Employment without a fixed duration is generally terminable by either party at will. Illinois recognizes a narrow retaliatory-discharge exception when termination violates clearly mandated public policy. Ordinary unfairness does not, by itself, establish that exception. — Turner v. Memorial Medical Center, 233 Ill. 2d 494 (2009).

facts.label: Workers’ compensation retaliation
facts.value: An employer may not discharge or threaten to discharge an employee because the employee exercises rights or remedies under the Workers’ Compensation Act. Illinois also recognizes a civil retaliatory-discharge claim for firing an employee for pursuing workers’ compensation rights. — 820 ILCS 305/4(h); Kelsay v. Motorola, Inc., 74 Ill. 2d 172 (1978).

rows: Covered employers cannot discharge employees because of protected characteristics, including race, religion, sex, age, disability, or sexual orientation.
Retaliation for opposing unlawful discrimination or participating in proceedings under the Illinois Human Rights Act is prohibited.

The Whistleblower Act protects specified disclosures based on a good-faith belief that an employer’s activity violates law or poses a substantial and specific danger to employees, public health, or safety.
Retaliation is prohibited when an employee refuses an activity the employee has a good-faith belief would violate state or federal law, rule, or regulation.
An employer cannot discharge, threaten to discharge, intimidate, or coerce an employee because of jury service.

facts.label: Handbooks can matter
facts.value: A handbook can create enforceable contractual rights when it contains a sufficiently clear promise, is disseminated so the employee knows its contents and reasonably understands it as an offer, and is accepted through starting or continuing work. Not every handbook creates a contract. — Duldulao v. Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital Center, 115 Ill. 2d 482 (1987).

facts.label: Final-pay deadline
facts.value: An employer must pay final compensation, if possible, at separation, but no later than the employee’s next regularly scheduled payday. Earned vacation must be paid when an employment contract or policy provides paid vacation; separation cannot trigger forfeiture of earned vacation. — 820 ILCS 115/5.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Illinois Department of Human Rights: investigates employment discrimination and retaliation charges under the Illinois Human Rights Act. The Illinois Human Rights Commission adjudicates administrative complaints.
Illinois Department of Labor: administers wage-payment complaints under the Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act, including unpaid final compensation.
Illinois circuit courts: hear common-law retaliatory-discharge lawsuits, employment-contract disputes, and civil actions authorized by the Illinois Whistleblower Act.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Must an employer give warnings first? At-will employment itself does not require progressive discipline; an enforceable agreement may change that result.
Does an unfair firing automatically support a lawsuit? No. The firing must implicate an applicable legal protection or enforceable contractual obligation.
Can an internal report receive whistleblower protection? Yes. Section 15 protects qualifying disclosures to a supervisor, principal officer, or qualifying supervisor of a contracting organization.
Does being fired eliminate earned vacation pay? No. Section 5 requires payment of earned vacation provided under the employer’s contract or policy.

employment-law/illinois/contractor-vs-em.summary: Illinois does not use one contractor-versus-employee test for every employment law: the governing standard depends on the work and the statute involved. The Employee Classification Act creates a specific employee presumption for construction work, while the Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act and Unemployment Insurance Act contain their own independent-contractor exclusions. A contractor agreement or Form 1099 does not, by itself, establish that a worker satisfies the applicable statutory test.

facts.label: Construction employee presumption
facts.value: An individual performing services for a contractor is deemed an employee under the Employee Classification Act unless the statutory independent-contractor test or qualifying sole-proprietor or partnership exception applies. The Act addresses construction, rather than all industries. — 820 ILCS 185/5 and 185/10.

facts.label: Wage-payment coverage
facts.value: The Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act excludes an individual from its employee definition only when all three statutory conditions concerning freedom from control, the location or nature of the services, and an independently established business are satisfied. — 820 ILCS 115/2.

facts.label: Unemployment insurance
facts.value: Services performed by an individual for an employing unit are deemed employment unless the employing unit establishes all three conditions in the unemployment statute's independent-contractor exception. — 820 ILCS 405/212.

rows: The individual must be free from control or direction, both under the contract and in fact.
Both statutes require freedom from control and direction under the contract and in fact.
The service must be outside the contractor's usual course of services.
Services must be outside the business's usual course or outside all its places of business.
The individual must be engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession, or business.
Wage law requires an independently established trade, occupation, profession, or business; unemployment law requires customary engagement in one.
A legitimate sole proprietor or partnership may qualify under the separate, multi-factor requirements of 820 ILCS 185/10(c).
Neither 820 ILCS 115/2 nor 820 ILCS 405/212 incorporates that construction-specific exception.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Illinois Department of Labor: administers the Employee Classification Act and handles complaints about construction-worker misclassification. — 820 ILCS 185/15 and 185/25.

Illinois Department of Labor: administers wage-payment complaints under the Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act. A classification dispute may arise when a business denies employee status in an unpaid-wage claim. — 820 ILCS 115/11.

Illinois Department of Employment Security: administers unemployment insurance, including determinations about whether services constitute employment under the Unemployment Insurance Act. — 820 ILCS 405/212.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Does receiving a Form 1099 settle my status? No. The cited Illinois statutes apply substantive conditions; a tax form alone does not establish freedom from control or an independently established business.

Does the construction law cover renovation and repairs? Yes. Its construction definition includes remodeling, repair, maintenance, rehabilitation, renovation, and demolition, among other activities. — 820 ILCS 185/5.

Is working away from the company's premises enough? No. Under the wage-payment and unemployment tests, working outside all places of business can satisfy one condition, but the control and independent-business conditions must also be met. — 820 ILCS 115/2; 820 ILCS 405/212.

Does passing one test settle every employment-law question? No. These statutes contain distinct coverage rules. Classification under one statute does not itself establish compliance with another; talk to a lawyer.

employment-law/illinois/non-compete-agre.summary: Illinois limits employment noncompete and nonsolicitation agreements under the Illinois Freedom to Work Act, with its principal modern restrictions applying to agreements entered into on or after January 1, 2022. In 2026, a noncompete is prohibited unless annualized earnings exceed $75,000, and a nonsolicitation agreement is prohibited unless earnings exceed $45,000. Exceeding those thresholds does not establish enforceability: consideration, legitimate business interests, reasonableness, and statutory notice requirements also matter.

facts.label: Noncompete agreements
facts.value: The Act covers agreements restricting work for another employer for a specified period, within a specified geographic area, or in similar work. It also includes agreements imposing adverse financial consequences for competitive activity after employment ends. — 820 ILCS 90/5.

facts.label: Nonsolicitation agreements
facts.value: The Act separately regulates restrictions on soliciting an employer’s employees and on soliciting or interfering with relationships involving clients, prospective clients, vendors, prospective vendors, suppliers, and prospective suppliers. — 820 ILCS 90/5.

facts.label: Excluded agreements
facts.value: The statutory definition of a noncompete excludes confidentiality agreements, restrictions on using or disclosing trade secrets, invention-assignment agreements, and covenants associated with buying or selling business goodwill or an ownership interest. These exclusions do not establish that every such agreement is enforceable. — 820 ILCS 90/5.

facts.label: Threshold rule
facts.value: Agreements prohibited by the earnings thresholds are illegal and void. Earnings include taxable compensation reflected or expected on Form W-2, including earned bonuses and commissions, plus specified employee elective deferrals. — 820 ILCS 90/5 and 90/10.

facts.label: Consideration
facts.value: Adequate consideration includes two years of employment after signing, or other sufficient consideration consisting of professional or financial benefits alone or combined with employment. — 820 ILCS 90/5.

facts.label: Business justification and scope
facts.value: An enforceable restriction must be ancillary to a valid employment relationship, no broader than necessary to protect a legitimate business interest, free of undue hardship on the employee, and not injurious to the public. Legitimate business interests depend on the totality of the circumstances. — 820 ILCS 90/15.

facts.label: Written notice and review period
facts.value: The employer must advise the employee in writing to consult an attorney. It must provide the covenant at least 14 calendar days before employment begins or provide at least 14 calendar days to review it; the employee may voluntarily sign sooner. — 820 ILCS 90/20.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Illinois circuit courts hear civil disputes over enforcement, subject to applicable jurisdiction and contractual dispute-resolution provisions.

The Illinois Attorney General may investigate and bring civil actions when there is reasonable cause to believe an employer has engaged in a pattern and practice prohibited by the Act. — 820 ILCS 90/30.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Is earning exactly $75,000 enough for a noncompete in 2026? No. The statute prohibits a noncompete when annualized earnings are equal to or below that amount. — 820 ILCS 90/10.
Does signing immediately defeat the agreement? Not necessarily. An employee may voluntarily sign before the review period ends if the employer satisfied the statutory requirements. — 820 ILCS 90/20.

Can an employee recover attorney fees? An employee who prevails on an employer’s civil complaint or arbitration claim to enforce a noncompete or nonsolicitation agreement must receive costs and reasonable attorney fees. — 820 ILCS 90/25.
Can a court narrow an excessive restriction? A court may reform or sever provisions in its discretion rather than invalidate the entire covenant, considering the statutory factors. — 820 ILCS 90/35.

employment-law/illinois/wage-theft.summary: Illinois wage-theft claims generally involve unpaid wages, missing overtime, unlawful deductions, or unpaid final compensation, including earned vacation owed under an employer’s policy. The Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act governs payment of agreed compensation, while the Illinois Minimum Wage Law establishes minimum-wage and overtime rights; depending on the violation, workers may pursue an Illinois Department of Labor claim or a civil lawsuit, with different deadlines and remedies.

facts.label: Agreed wages
facts.value: The Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act covers compensation owed under an employment contract or agreement. Its definition of wages includes compensation calculated by time, task, piece, or another method; an agreement need not necessarily be a formal written contract. — 820 ILCS 115/2

facts.label: Minimum wage and overtime
facts.value: The Illinois Minimum Wage Law generally requires covered adult employees to receive at least $15 per hour. Covered, nonexempt employees generally must receive at least 1.5 times their regular rate for hours exceeding 40 in a workweek. Statutory exceptions apply. — 820 ILCS 105/4, 4a

facts.label: Deductions
facts.value: Wage deductions are restricted. Permitted categories include deductions required by law, deductions benefiting the employee, valid wage assignments or deduction orders, and deductions made with the employee’s express written consent given freely when the deduction is made. — 820 ILCS 115/9

rows: Wages generally must be paid at least semimonthly; statutory exceptions permit some employees to be paid monthly.
Final compensation is due at separation if possible, and no later than the next regularly scheduled payday.
When an employment contract or policy provides paid vacation, earned unused vacation must be included in final compensation. A policy cannot forfeit earned vacation at separation.
A complaint under the Wage Payment and Collection Act must be filed with the Department of Labor within one year after the wages or final compensation became due.
An employee’s civil action under the Minimum Wage Law must be brought within three years after the underpayment.

facts.label: Wage-payment damages
facts.value: Employees may recover unpaid wages or final compensation plus damages equal to 5% of the underpayment for each month it remains unpaid. In a civil action, employees may also recover costs and reasonable attorney fees. — 820 ILCS 115/14(a)

facts.label: Minimum-wage remedies
facts.value: The Minimum Wage Law authorizes a civil recovery of three times the underpayment, costs, reasonable attorney fees, and additional statutory monthly damages. — 820 ILCS 105/12(a)

facts.label: Protected complaints
facts.value: The Wage Payment and Collection Act prohibits discharge or other discrimination for protected wage complaints, proceedings, or testimony. Its retaliation provision authorizes reinstatement, lost compensation, costs, and reasonable attorney fees. — 820 ILCS 115/14(c)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: The Illinois Department of Labor accepts unpaid-wage and final-compensation complaints under the Wage Payment and Collection Act, and minimum-wage and overtime complaints under the Minimum Wage Law.

Illinois circuit courts hear civil wage-recovery lawsuits. The Wage Payment and Collection Act permits an employee to pursue its civil remedy without first exhausting the Department’s administrative process. — 820 ILCS 115/14(a)

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Does quitting eliminate the right to a final paycheck? No. Final-compensation requirements apply to employees who resign as well as those discharged. — 820 ILCS 115/2, 5
Can an employer withhold all pay during a wage dispute? No. The employer must timely pay the amount it concedes is due, without conditions. — 820 ILCS 115/9
Does receiving a salary automatically eliminate overtime? No. Overtime coverage depends on applicable statutory requirements and exemptions, not salary status alone. — 820 ILCS 105/4a

Are independent contractors covered by the Wage Payment and Collection Act? The Act excludes individuals meeting its statutory independent-contractor criteria; a contractor label alone does not establish that exclusion. — 820 ILCS 115/2

employment-law/illinois/unemployment-ben.summary: Illinois unemployment insurance provides temporary benefits to eligible workers under the Illinois Unemployment Insurance Act, administered by the Illinois Department of Employment Security (IDES). Eligibility depends on covered earnings, the circumstances of separation, and continuing requirements such as being able and available for work; a layoff does not automatically establish entitlement, and quitting or being discharged does not automatically resolve the claim. Claimants and employers can challenge IDES decisions through administrative appeals, with judicial review available after a final administrative decision.

facts.label: Governing law and agency
facts.value: The Illinois Unemployment Insurance Act governs state unemployment benefits. IDES administers claims and determines whether a claimant satisfies the Act’s monetary and nonmonetary requirements. — 820 ILCS 405.

facts.label: Weekly eligibility
facts.value: Eligibility is determined for individual weeks. The Act includes requirements concerning registration for work, claims for benefits, ability to work, availability for work, and actively seeking work, subject to statutory exceptions. — 820 ILCS 405/500.

facts.label: Earnings requirement
facts.value: A claimant must satisfy the Act’s qualifying-wage requirements based on covered earnings in the applicable base period. Losing a job, by itself, does not establish monetary eligibility. — 820 ILCS 405/500(E).

facts.label: Continuing claims
facts.value: An initial application and continuing claims serve different purposes: continuing claims establish eligibility for the weeks for which benefits are requested. A claimant may meet the initial earnings requirement but be ineligible for a particular week. — 820 ILCS 405/500.

sections.heading: How common employment situations affect benefits

rows: The claimant must still meet the Act’s earnings and weekly eligibility requirements.
Leaving voluntarily without good cause attributable to the employing unit generally disqualifies a claimant, subject to statutory exceptions.
Discharge for misconduct connected with work can disqualify a claimant. The employer’s decision to fire someone is not itself the statutory test.
Failing without good cause to apply for or accept suitable work can cause disqualification; suitability is evaluated under statutory factors.
The Act generally requires ability and availability for work for the week claimed, subject to its exceptions.

facts.label: Appealing an initial determination
facts.value: An appeal from a claims adjudicator’s determination generally must be filed within 30 calendar days after delivery or mailing of the notice. The administrative appeal proceeds before a referee. — 820 ILCS 405/800.

facts.label: Board of Review
facts.value: A referee’s decision may be appealed to the IDES Board of Review within 30 calendar days after the decision is mailed. — 820 ILCS 405/801.

facts.label: Court review
facts.value: Final Board of Review decisions are subject to the Administrative Review Law. An administrative-review action generally must be commenced within 35 days after service of the decision. — 820 ILCS 405/1100; 735 ILCS 5/3-103.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: IDES receives unemployment insurance claims and administers benefit determinations under the Illinois Unemployment Insurance Act.
Challenges to claims adjudicator determinations proceed through IDES administrative appeals; referee decisions are reviewed by the Board of Review.
Illinois circuit courts hear administrative-review actions challenging final Board of Review decisions. These are judicial-review proceedings, not new unemployment applications.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Can someone receive benefits after quitting? Sometimes. Section 601 contains exceptions to the general voluntary-leaving disqualification.
Does every firing disqualify a worker? No. Section 602 addresses misconduct connected with work, not every reason an employer might terminate employment.
Must a claimant accept any offered job? No. Section 603 addresses suitable work and recognizes good cause for refusal.
Can an employer appeal an award? Yes. Section 800 provides appeal rights to claimants and qualifying employing units.

employment-law/indiana/wrongful-terminat.summary: Indiana generally follows at-will employment: an employer may discharge an employee without proving good cause, but not for a reason prohibited by law or an enforceable employment agreement. Wrongful-termination claims can involve discrimination, retaliation, breach of contract, or narrow public-policy exceptions recognized by Indiana courts, including retaliation for exercising workers’ compensation rights. The applicable deadline and forum depend on the claim; Indiana Civil Rights Commission discrimination complaints generally must be filed within 180 days of the alleged discriminatory act.

sections.heading: When termination can be unlawful in Indiana

facts.label: At-will employment
facts.value: Employment without a definite or ascertainable term is presumptively at will. Indiana recognizes limited exceptions; unfair treatment alone does not necessarily establish wrongful discharge. — Orr v. Westminster Village North, Inc., 689 N.E.2d 712 (Ind. 1997)

facts.label: Workers’ compensation retaliation
facts.value: Indiana recognizes a wrongful-discharge claim when an employee is fired in retaliation for exercising rights under the workers’ compensation system. This is a judicially recognized exception to at-will employment. — Frampton v. Central Indiana Gas Co., 297 N.E.2d 425 (Ind. 1973)

facts.label: Refusing an unlawful act
facts.value: Indiana recognizes a narrow exception where an employee is discharged for refusing to commit an illegal act for which the employee would be personally liable. — McClanahan v. Remington Freight Lines, Inc., 517 N.E.2d 390 (Ind. 1988)

facts.label: Discriminatory termination
facts.value: The Indiana Civil Rights Law prohibits covered employment discrimination based on race, religion, color, sex, disability, national origin, or ancestry. Its employer definition generally reaches employers with six or more employees, subject to statutory exclusions. — Indiana Code §§ 22-9-1-2, 22-9-1-3, 22-9-1-6

rows: An ICRC complaint generally must be filed within 180 days after the alleged discriminatory practice.
For discrimination covered by both federal law and an applicable state or local prohibition, the EEOC charge deadline generally extends to 300 days; coverage and exceptions matter.
Employment-related lawsuit without a written contract
Indiana generally requires actions relating to employment terms, conditions, or privileges, except actions based on a written contract, within two years of the challenged act or omission.
Earned wages generally are payable on the regular payday for the pay period in which separation occurred, rather than immediately upon discharge.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Indiana
bullets: Indiana Civil Rights Commission: investigates employment-discrimination complaints under the Indiana Civil Rights Law. State administrative coverage and deadlines differ from federal requirements. — Indiana Code § 22-9-1-6

U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: receives federal employment-discrimination charges, including charges alleging discriminatory discharge or retaliation for protected discrimination complaints. — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5

Indiana trial courts: hear civil wrongful-discharge and contract claims within their jurisdiction. Federal employment claims may also proceed in the U.S. District Courts for the Northern or Southern District of Indiana when jurisdictional and procedural requirements are satisfied.

Indiana Department of Labor: administers the wage-claim process for qualifying unpaid-wage claims. Recovering earned wages is separate from proving the termination itself unlawful. — Indiana Code § 22-2-9-4

sections.heading: Common questions in Indiana
bullets: Must an employer give a reason for firing someone? Generally, at-will employment does not require good cause, but a prohibited motive can make the discharge unlawful.

Does an employee handbook automatically guarantee continued employment? No. Whether handbook language creates enforceable contractual rights depends on contract principles and the document’s terms. — Orr, 689 N.E.2d 712
Can filing for workers’ compensation support a retaliation claim? Yes. Indiana recognizes retaliatory discharge for exercising workers’ compensation rights. — Frampton, 297 N.E.2d 425
Does every wrongful-termination claim require an EEOC charge? No. Federal discrimination procedures differ from state common-law wrongful-discharge claims and contract actions.

employment-law/iowa/family-medical-leave.summary: Iowa does not have a general state paid family and medical leave program, but eligible employees can receive unpaid, job-protected leave under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). Iowa law separately requires covered employers to provide limited leave for pregnancy-related disability when other available leave is insufficient. These protections differ in employer coverage, employee eligibility, qualifying reasons, and duration; federal pregnancy-accommodation law can also require leave in appropriate circumstances.

facts.label: State entitlement
facts.value: When sufficient leave is unavailable under an employer’s health or temporary disability insurance or sick leave plan, an employee is entitled to leave for pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions for the period of disability or eight weeks, whichever is shorter. This is not a general eight-week parental bonding benefit. — Iowa Code § 216.6(2)(e)

facts.label: Employer coverage
facts.value: Iowa’s employment-discrimination provisions generally exclude employers that regularly employ fewer than four individuals. Other statutory exclusions also apply. — Iowa Code § 216.6(6)

facts.label: Notice and certification
facts.value: The employee must give timely notice of the period requested, and the employer must approve a change in that period before it becomes effective. The employer may require medical certification that the employee cannot reasonably perform employment duties. — Iowa Code § 216.6(2)(e)

facts.label: Equal treatment
facts.value: Written and unwritten employment policies must treat pregnancy-related disabilities as temporary disabilities for employment-related purposes, including leave and benefits. — Iowa Code § 216.6(2)

rows: Private employers generally need 50 employees for at least 20 workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Public agencies and elementary and secondary schools are covered regardless of size.
Generally requires 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours worked during the preceding 12 months, and 50 employees within 75 miles of the worksite.
Up to 12 workweeks in a 12-month period for qualifying reasons, including a serious health condition, care for a spouse, child, or parent, and birth or placement of a child.
Up to 26 workweeks in a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember, subject to eligibility and relationship requirements.
The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act generally covers employers with at least 15 employees. Leave may be a reasonable accommodation unless it causes undue hardship.

sections.heading: Pay, benefits, and return to work

facts.label: Pay and overlapping leave
facts.value: FMLA leave is generally unpaid, although qualifying accrued paid leave may run concurrently under applicable rules. Iowa’s pregnancy-leave provision does not itself require paid leave. — 29 U.S.C. § 2612(c)–(d); Iowa Code § 216.6(2)(e)

facts.label: Federal job protection
facts.value: FMLA generally requires continued group health coverage on the same terms and restoration to the same or an equivalent position. Interference and retaliation are prohibited. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 2614–2615

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Iowa
bullets: Iowa Office of Civil Rights: Employment-discrimination complaints under the Iowa Civil Rights Act generally must be filed within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory practice. — Iowa Code § 216.15(13)
U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: Handles FMLA complaints. A private FMLA lawsuit generally must be filed within two years, or three years for a willful violation. — 29 U.S.C. § 2617
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: Handles federal pregnancy-discrimination and Pregnant Workers Fairness Act charges.

sections.heading: Common questions in Iowa
bullets: Does Iowa guarantee paid parental leave for all employees? No. Neither Iowa’s pregnancy-disability provision nor the FMLA creates that universal entitlement.
Does Iowa’s eight-week provision cover fathers bonding with a newborn? No. It addresses pregnancy-related disability, not general bonding leave; eligible fathers can qualify for FMLA bonding leave.
Can FMLA leave be taken intermittently? Yes, when medically necessary for qualifying conditions. Intermittent bonding leave generally requires employer agreement. — 29 U.S.C. § 2612(b)

Can an employer force pregnancy leave instead of an accommodation? Under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, an employer cannot require leave if another reasonable accommodation can be provided. — 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg-1(4)

employment-law/iowa/unemployment-benefit.summary: Iowa unemployment benefits are administered by Iowa Workforce Development and depend on covered wages, the reason employment ended, and continuing eligibility during each claimed week. Regular benefits are generally limited to 16 weeks, and workers ordinarily must be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work. Quitting without good cause attributable to the employer, discharge for misconduct, or refusing suitable work can disqualify a claimant, subject to statutory exceptions and the circumstances of the case.

sections.heading: Eligibility and benefit limits in Iowa

facts.label: Covered wages
facts.value: Eligibility requires sufficient insured wages during the base period. Iowa generally defines the base period as the first four of the last five completed calendar quarters before the benefit year begins. Meeting the wage requirement does not by itself establish eligibility. — Iowa Code §§ 96.19(3), 96.4(4)

facts.label: Weekly eligibility
facts.value: A claimant generally must register for work, make a claim, and be able to work, available for work, and earnestly and actively seeking work. Statutory exceptions apply to certain claimants and circumstances. — Iowa Code § 96.4(1)–(3)

facts.label: Benefit amount and duration
facts.value: The weekly benefit calculation depends on covered wages and qualifying dependents, subject to statutory maximums. Regular benefits are generally capped at 16 times the weekly benefit amount; the base-period wage limitation can produce a smaller total entitlement. — Iowa Code § 96.3(4)–(5)

sections.heading: How the reason for unemployment affects benefits

rows: A layoff does not remove the separate wage, claim-filing, and weekly eligibility requirements.
Leaving voluntarily without good cause attributable to the employer generally disqualifies the worker, but statutory exceptions exist.
Discharge for misconduct connected with employment can disqualify the worker. Being fired does not automatically establish misconduct.
Failure without good cause to apply for or accept suitable work can disqualify a claimant. Suitability depends on statutory factors.
Reduced-hours work may qualify for partial benefits, but earnings affect the amount payable.

facts.label: Initial appeal deadline
facts.value: An initial benefits determination generally becomes final unless an interested party appeals within ten calendar days after notification is mailed to the party’s last-known address. This is the initial-determination deadline, not a universal deadline for every review stage. — Iowa Code § 96.6(2)

facts.label: Overpayment recovery
facts.value: Benefits paid to someone later found ineligible are generally recoverable even when the claimant acted in good faith. Iowa law contains exceptions, including a limited exception involving certain reversed separation decisions and employer participation. — Iowa Code § 96.3(7)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Iowa
bullets: Iowa Workforce Development administers unemployment claims, benefit determinations, and claimant services. Its official unemployment website provides the claim-filing entry point.
Iowa Workforce Development’s unemployment appeals process handles challenges to initial benefit determinations under Iowa Code § 96.6.
Iowa district courts conduct judicial review of qualifying final agency decisions under Iowa Code § 17A.19.

sections.heading: Common questions in Iowa
bullets: Does every unemployed worker receive 16 weeks? No. Sixteen weeks is the general regular-benefit ceiling; wage-based limits and ongoing eligibility can reduce benefits.
Can someone receive benefits after being fired? Yes, potentially. Iowa distinguishes discharge from disqualifying misconduct connected with employment.
Does quitting always prevent benefits? No. The voluntary-quit statute includes exceptions, and whether good cause is attributable to the employer matters.
Can part-time earnings affect benefits? Yes. Iowa’s partial-benefit rules account for earnings when determining the weekly payment.

employment-law/kansas/overtime-rights.summary: Kansas overtime rights depend on which law covers the employment: the federal Fair Labor Standards Act generally requires overtime after 40 hours in a workweek, while the Kansas Minimum Wage and Maximum Hours Law generally uses a 46-hour threshold for covered employment outside federal coverage. Both generally require time-and-a-half for covered, nonexempt overtime hours, but coverage and exemptions determine whether either rule applies; Kansas does not generally require overtime merely because someone works more than eight hours in a day.

sections.heading: Which overtime law applies in Kansas

facts.label: Federal coverage comes first
facts.value: The Kansas law’s definition of employer excludes employers subject to the federal Fair Labor Standards Act. The state’s 46-hour rule is therefore not a replacement for the federal 40-hour requirement at federally covered employers. — K.S.A. 44-1202; 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1)

facts.label: Kansas overtime requirement
facts.value: For employment covered by the Kansas overtime provision, an employer generally must pay at least one and one-half times the employee’s hourly wage rate for hours worked beyond 46 in a workweek. Statutory exclusions and exceptions apply. — K.S.A. 44-1204

facts.label: Federal overtime requirement
facts.value: Covered, nonexempt employees generally receive at least one and one-half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. The regular rate can include compensation beyond the stated hourly wage, including certain bonuses. — 29 U.S.C. § 207(a), (e)

facts.label: Salaried employees
facts.value: A salary alone does not establish a federal overtime exemption. Executive, administrative and professional exemptions depend on applicable duties and compensation requirements, not simply a job title. — 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1); 29 C.F.R. Part 541

rows: Overtime generally begins after 40 hours worked in one workweek. — 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1)
Employment covered by Kansas overtime law
Overtime generally begins after 46 hours worked in one workweek. — K.S.A. 44-1204
Neither general overtime rule uses an eight-hour daily trigger. — K.S.A. 44-1204; 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1)
Each workweek stands alone; hours generally cannot be averaged across two weeks to avoid overtime. — 29 C.F.R. § 778.104
A workweek is a fixed, regularly recurring period of 168 hours, consisting of seven consecutive 24-hour periods. — 29 C.F.R. § 778.105

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kansas
bullets: The Kansas Department of Labor’s Employment Standards unit handles state wage complaints and administers Kansas wage-and-hour laws. Federal coverage affects whether the Kansas overtime provision applies. — K.S.A. 44-1202, 44-1204.
The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division receives complaints about federal overtime violations involving employment in Kansas. — 29 U.S.C. § 211.

Federal overtime claims may also be brought in a state or federal court with jurisdiction. The usual federal limitations period is two years, extended to three years for willful violations; recovery can include unpaid overtime, an equal amount in liquidated damages, and attorney fees. — 29 U.S.C. §§ 216(b), 255(a), 260.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kansas
bullets: Does Kansas let every employer wait until 46 hours to pay overtime? No. Federally covered, nonexempt employment generally follows the 40-hour federal threshold. — K.S.A. 44-1202; 29 U.S.C. § 207.
Is Sunday or holiday work automatically overtime? No. Weekend or holiday work alone does not trigger these statutory overtime requirements. — K.S.A. 44-1204; 29 C.F.R. § 778.102.

Can a private employer replace federally required overtime with time off in a later week? Generally no. Federal law provides a separate compensatory-time arrangement for qualifying state and local public employment. — 29 U.S.C. § 207(a), (o).
Can an employer retaliate over a federal overtime complaint? The FLSA prohibits retaliation for protected complaints or participation in proceedings under the Act. — 29 U.S.C. § 215(a)(3).
